name: Arrack Punch
variant: Single-serve spec, Boothby's The World's Drinks (1908)

ingredients.orig: a large spoonful of sugar ('this punch needs much sweetening')

source: William 'Cocktail' Boothby, The World's Drinks and How to Mix Them (1908), No. 327
notes: Batavia arrack punch is the original Anglo-Indian punch that sailors carried west in the 1600s; rum later displaced arrack in the Caribbean. Boothby's measures are explicit except the loose 'large spoonful' of sugar, so the sweetness here is an interpretation; Jerry Thomas (1862) gives the older bowl form as 3 parts arrack to 2 of rum, lemons, 'a good deal' of sugar and 6 parts water.

name: Fish House Punch
variant: Philadelphia Fish-House Punch, Jerry Thomas (1862) bowl recipe
garnish: large block of ice in the bowl
source: Jerry Thomas, How to Mix Drinks / Bar-Tender's Guide (1862), No. 46
notes: The house punch of a Philadelphia gentlemen's fishing club founded in 1732; the classic three-spirit blend (cognac, peach brandy, Jamaica rum) is diluted heavily with water, the template for later multi-spirit tiki bowls. Historic peach brandy was a drier aged fruit brandy, mapped here to peach liqueur (the usual modern stand-in).

name: Grog
variant: Difford's single-serve after Admiral Vernon's 1740 ration
creator: Admiral Edward Vernon (ration order)
source: Difford's Guide, 'Grog' (history: Vernon's 1740 order cutting the half-pint ration with water, 4:1)
notes: In 1740 Admiral Vernon ('Old Grogram') ordered the half-pint daily rum ration served in two portions diluted with four parts water, with lime and sugar allowed to make it palatable. The historical ration was far weaker than this modern single serve; Donn Beach's Navy Grog is its luxurious descendant.

name: Barbados Rum Punch
variant: Traditional Bajan 1-2-3-4 formula
source: Barbadian tradition ('one of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak'); same 1-2-3-4 formula in Charles H. Baker, The Gentleman's Companion Vol. II (1939)
notes: Barbados keeps the old rum-punch rhyme as a national recipe: one part lime, two of syrup, three of rum, four of water, with Angostura and nutmeg. It is the skeleton every Planter's Punch and most tiki punches hang on; one part = 1/2 oz here.

name: Jamaican Rum Punch
variant: 1-2-3-4 formula with Jamaican white overproof rum (Difford's Guide 'Rum Punch')
source: Difford's Guide, 'Rum Punch' (classic 1:2:3:4 proportions)
notes: Jamaica's rum punch follows the same sour-sweet-strong-weak rhyme but is built on fiery white overproof rum, which makes a much hotter drink than the Barbadian version. Island versions often swap part of the water for fruit juices and strawberry or sorrel syrup.

name: Regent's Punch
variant: Bordeaux Wine & Liquor Dealers' Guide (1857), reprinted by Jerry Thomas (1862)
garnish: sliced pineapple steeped in the bowl
source: The Bordeaux Wine and Liquor Dealers' Guide (1857), Appendix 'Regent's Punch'; Jerry Thomas (1862) No. 31
notes: A Regency-era party bowl said to honor George IV as Prince Regent: rum, brandy and arrack together with curaçao, tea, citrus and champagne, finished with fresh pineapple. The 1857 source gives 1 1/2 pints of the tea, lemon and capillaire (Jerry Thomas's reprint lost the fraction); green tea is mapped to brewed black tea.

name: Hot Buttered Rum
variant: 'Hot Spiced Rum', Jerry Thomas (1862)

ingredients.orig: 1 piece of butter as large as half a chestnut

source: Jerry Thomas, How to Mix Drinks (1862), No. 207 'Hot Spiced Rum'
notes: Colonial America's winter rum: Jamaica rum, sugar, allspice and cloves, a knob of butter and boiling water. Trader Vic and Don the Beachcomber later sold batter-based versions; allspice is noted in orig since only cloves map to the vocabulary.

name: Knickerbocker
variant: Jerry Thomas (1862)

ingredients.orig: 1/2 a lime or lemon, juice and rind in the glass

source: Jerry Thomas, How to Mix Drinks (1862), No. 184
notes: A mid-19th-century 'fancy' rum drink: St. Croix rum, lime shell and juice, raspberry syrup and curaçao shaken with shaved ice and served with the ice and berries. Beachbum Berry points to it as a proto-tiki drink — fruit syrup plus orange liqueur plus rum and lime.

name: Canchánchara
variant: IBA official spec

ingredients.orig: 15 ml raw honey (≈1 oz 1:1 honey mix)
50 ml water (reduced for the honey conversion)

source: IBA official cocktail list (New Era Drinks)
notes: Cane aguardiente, raw honey, lime and water stirred in a clay cup — the drink associated with Cuba's independence fighters (mambises) of the 1860s–90s and a folk ancestor of the Daiquiri. Honey is converted to the 1:1 honey mix used across this dataset.

name: Ti' Punch
variant: Smuggler's Cove spec

ingredients.orig: 2 oz AOC Martinique rhum agricole blanc
1 chunk (coin) of fresh lime, squeezed and dropped in

source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove (2016)
notes: The French Antilles' 'little punch': grassy cane-juice rhum with a spoon of cane syrup and a squeezed coin of lime, usually no ice, each drinker building his own. Lafcadio Hearn recorded it in Martinique around 1890. The lime amount is an estimate of one squeezed disc.

name: Pisco Punch
variant: After John Lannes's recipe (Difford's adaptation)
creator: Duncan Nicol

ingredients.orig: 30 ml pineapple juice (stand-in for pineapple-gum-syrup marinade)

source: Difford's Guide, 'Pisco Punch (Lannes' recipe)'
notes: Duncan Nicol's secret Gold Coast punch of Peruvian pisco and pineapple gum syrup made San Francisco's Bank Exchange famous; every modern spec is a reconstruction (Lannes, Micheli and Prosser versions all differ). It shows the Bay Area pineapple-and-spirit taste Trader Vic grew up with.

name: Daiquiri
variant: Original Cox/Stout mixture as recorded by Charles H. Baker (1939)
creator: Jennings Cox & Harry E. Stout

ingredients.orig: 1 whisky glass level full of Bacardi Carta Blanca (or Carta de Oro)
juice of 1 1/2 small green limes, strained

source: Charles H. Baker Jr., The Gentleman's Companion Vol. II (1939), 'The One & Only Tropical Daiquiri'
notes: Baker credits American mining engineers Jennings Cox and Harry Stout (summer 1898) with lacing boiled drinking water with Bacardi, lime and sugar; the mixture is shaken hard with fine ice and poured unstrained. Baker himself advises cutting the sugar to 1 tsp.

name: Daiquiri
variant: IBA official spec
source: IBA official cocktail list (The Unforgettables)
notes: Rum, lime and sugar shaken and served up — punch concentrated into a sour. It is the chassis for Donn Beach's flash-blended rum drinks and, through Trader Vic, the Mai Tai.

name: Cuba Libre
variant: Sloppy Joe's Bar, Havana (1940 manual)
source: Sloppy Joe's Bar Cocktails Manual (Havana, season 1940); cf. Zabriskie (1948), Baker (1939)
notes: Rum, lime and Coca-Cola, said to date from the years just after 1898. Baker complained it was too sweet and muddled the lime peel to add bitterness; the lime is what separates it from a plain rum-and-coke.

name: Planter's Punch
variant: 1908 New York Times rhyme ('two of sour, one and a half of sweet, three of strong, four of weak')
source: Verse printed in The New York Times, 8 August 1908 (as quoted by Ted Haigh and others)
notes: The earliest printed Planter's Punch is a rhyme rather than a recipe card: it tilts the Caribbean formula toward the sour (two of lime to one and a half of sweet) around three parts of Jamaican rum. One part = 1/2 oz here; the sweetener type is not specified, so rich syrup is an interpretation. Donn Beach's first menu was essentially this drink exploded into variations.

name: Bacardi Cocktail
variant: Grenadine version, 'Lest We Forget' (1933); earliest grenadine print Jacques Straub (1914)
source: Lest We Forget (1933); Jacques Straub, Drinks (1914)
notes: A pink Daiquiri sweetened with grenadine that became so popular in the 1930s that a 1936 New York court ruled it must be made with Bacardi. Some early books (Ensslin 1917) print it as a plain Daiquiri with gum syrup.

name: El Presidente
variant: Club de Cantineros de la República de Cuba manual (1930)
source: Manual Oficial, Club de Cantineros de la República de Cuba (1930); same in El Arte del Cantinero (1948)
notes: Havana's answer to the Manhattan, first recorded in a 1915 Cuban bartender's manual: equal rum and Chambéry-style vermouth, stirred and pinked with grenadine. Chambéry blanc is mapped to dry vermouth.

name: Presidente Menocal Special
variant: Bar La Florida (1934–1939)
source: Cocktails Bar La Florida (Havana, 1934, 1935, 1939 eds.)
notes: A Cuban rum julep named for President Mario García Menocal (1913–21): mint crushed with sugar and a few drops of lime, Bacardi, and a glass packed with crushed ice. It sits between the Mojito and the mint-bouquet swizzles; 'several drops' of lime is recorded as 1 tsp.

name: Singapore Sling
variant: Raffles Hotel 'original formula' as recorded by Charles H. Baker (met 1926, pub. 1939)
creator: Ngiam Tong Boon (attributed)

ingredients.orig: fill to taste with chilled club soda (10 oz highball)

source: Charles H. Baker Jr., The Gentleman's Companion Vol. II: An Exotic Drinking Book (1939)
notes: Baker's account of the Raffles sling is equal parts gin, cherry brandy and Bénédictine lengthened with soda — no citrus or pineapple. It shows the colonial Far-East sling before the fruit-juice punch version took over; soda volume is 'to taste'.

name: Singapore Sling
variant: Raffles Hotel / IBA modern formula (with pineapple)
creator: Ngiam Tong Boon (attributed)
source: IBA official cocktail list (Contemporary Classics); Difford's 'Raffles Formula'
notes: Today's Raffles/IBA sling is a long pineapple punch seasoned with cherry, orange and herbal liqueurs, grenadine and bitters — structurally a resort tropical. The pineapple-heavy formula almost certainly postdates Baker's 1920s equal-parts sling; year reflects the drink's origin.

name: Doctor Cocktail
variant: Swedish punsch and lime (Ensslin 1917; UKBG 1937 proportions)

ingredients.orig: 1/3 lemon or fresh lime juice (Ensslin: juice of 1 lime)

source: Hugo R. Ensslin, Recipes for Mixed Drinks (1917); U.K.B.G. Approved Cocktails (1937)
notes: Swedish punsch — a bottled descendant of the old Batavia arrack punch — simply soured with lime. Trader Vic reprinted a Doctor (1947), and punsch-and-lime drinks inspired later tiki riffs like the Doctor Funk.

name: Caipirinha
variant: IBA official spec

ingredients.orig: 1 lime cut into small wedges, muddled

source: IBA official cocktail list (Contemporary Classics)
notes: Brazil's national drink: lime wedges muddled with sugar so the peel oils join the juice, then cachaça over cracked ice. Origin stories point to the São Paulo countryside around the 1918 flu epidemic; the lime yield of muddled wedges is estimated.

name: Dark 'n Stormy
variant: IBA official spec
source: IBA official cocktail list (New Era Drinks)
notes: Bermuda's black rum floated on spicy ginger beer — a trademark of Gosling's, whose lore places it just after World War I. It is the template for the rum-and-ginger tiki coolers.

name: Queen's Park Swizzle
variant: Smuggler's Cove spec
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove (2016)
notes: The signature of Trinidad's Queen's Park Hotel (opened 1895): dark Demerara-style rum, lime, demerara sugar and mint swizzled until the glass frosts, then crowned with Angostura. Trader Vic printed it in 1946–47 and praised it lavishly, carrying it into the tiki canon.

name: West Indian Swizzle
variant: Angostura Bitters Centenary Gift Book (Trinidad, 1924)

ingredients.orig: half wineglass brandy or Jamaica rum
one teaspoonful Dr. Siegert's Angostura Bitters

source: Angostura Bitters Centenary Gift Book of Cocktail and Other Recipes (1924); cf. Bird & Turner, Cocktails: Their Kicks and Side-Kicks (1933) 'Rum Swizzle'
notes: The old Caribbean bitters swizzle: spirit, sugar and a whole teaspoon of Angostura beaten with half a wineglass of crushed ice until the ice melts, then poured off. Bird & Turner (1933) give the same no-citrus pitcher formula and trace the Rum Swizzle to Demerara.

name: Mary Pickford
variant: Hollywood Cocktails (1933) spec
source: Hollywood Cocktails (1933); same spec in UKBG Approved Cocktails (1937); Club de Cantineros manual (1930) omits the maraschino
notes: A Prohibition-era Havana tribute to the silent-film star: equal rum and pineapple tinted with grenadine and a whisper of maraschino, no citrus. The rum-pineapple-grenadine core is a straight line to Don the Beachcomber's pineapple drinks.

name: Air Mail
variant: Difford's Guide spec (after Bacardi pamphlet, 1930s; Esquire, 1949)

ingredients.orig: 30 ml light gold rum (Bacardi Gold in the Bacardi leaflet)
15 ml 3:1 honey syrup (≈0.8 oz 1:1 honey mix)

source: Difford's Guide, 'Air Mail' (history: 1930s Bacardi pamphlet 'Bacardi and Its Many Uses'; Whitfield 1941; Embury 1948; Esquire 1949)
notes: A honey Daiquiri with gold rum topped with champagne and served tall over ice — honey-sweetened rum sours like this lead straight to Donn Beach's 'honey mix' drinks.

name: Isle of Pines
variant: Cuban Cookery (Havana, 1931)
source: Blanche Z. de Baralt, Cuban Cookery (1931); also 'Jimmy' of Ciro's, Cocktails (1930) and Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Book (1935)
notes: Named for Cuba's grapefruit-growing Isla de Pinos: a Daiquiri in which grapefruit replaces the lime, barely sweetened. Grapefruit as a rum partner runs from here to the Hemingway, the Navy Grog and Don's Mix.

name: Mojito
variant: 'Mojito Criollo No. 1', Bar La Florida (1934)

ingredients.orig: several sprigs of mint, bruised in the glass
peel of one lime with its juice squeezed into the glass
sparkling water to fill an 8 oz glass

source: Cocktails Bar La Florida (Havana, 1934; 1935 ed.); same build in Sloppy Joe's Bar manuals (1931–1940) and Club de Cantineros (1930)
notes: Havana's rum highball: lime shell and juice, sugar and mint stirred so the mint gives up its juice, then rum and sparkling water, served unstrained over cracked ice. Printed by Havana bars from the early 1930s; folk ancestry is traced to the older 'Draque'.

name: Bermuda Rum Swizzle
variant: Swizzle Inn style (Difford's Guide, via Del Pedro)
source: Difford's Guide, 'Bermuda Rum Swizzle' (adapted from Del Pedro's Swizzle Inn recipe)
notes: Bermuda's national drink as poured at the Swizzle Inn (founded 1932): Gosling's gold and black rums with pineapple, orange and lemon-lime juices, falernum and Angostura, swizzled by the pitcher. The juicier, falernum-spiced style anticipates the resort punches.

name: Daiquiri No. 1
variant: Bar La Florida (El Floridita), Havana — 1934/1939 menu books
creator: Constantino Ribalaigua Vert
source: Cocktails Bar La Florida (Havana, 1934; 1939 'Cuña del Daiquiri' ed.)
notes: Constante's base Daiquiri: two ounces of Bacardi, a teaspoon of sugar and half a lime, shaken with cracked ice and strained. By modern standards it is very dry and rum-forward.

name: Daiquiri No. 2
variant: Bar La Florida (El Floridita), Havana — 1934/1939 menu books
creator: Constantino Ribalaigua Vert
source: Cocktails Bar La Florida (Havana, 1934; 1939 ed.)
notes: Gold Bacardi with an orange accent from curaçao and a spoon of orange juice. 'Several dashes' of curaçao is recorded as 4 dashes.

name: Daiquiri No. 3
variant: Bar La Florida (El Floridita) — 'Maidique Style' (1934) / 'B. Orbón' (1935–37) / 'Floridita Special' (1939)
creator: Constantino Ribalaigua Vert
source: Cocktails Bar La Florida (Havana, 1934, 1935, 1937, 1939 eds.)
notes: The grapefruit-and-maraschino Daiquiri that became the Hemingway's template; unlike the others it calls for a tablespoon (cucharada) of sugar in every edition, and is shaken with frappé ice and served frappé.

name: Daiquiri No. 4
variant: Bar La Florida (El Floridita) 'Florida Style' — the frappé Daiquiri
creator: Constantino Ribalaigua Vert
source: Cocktails Bar La Florida (1934, 1937, 1939 eds.), incl. Jack Cuddy's 1937 interview with Constante
notes: Constante's signature: shaken on a drugstore spindle mixer with ice shaved 'almost to snow' for about three minutes, then strained through a coarse strainer into chilled glasses. This electric-mixer frappé technique is the direct ancestor of Donn Beach's flash-blending.

name: El Presidente
variant: Bar La Florida (1934) — curaçao instead of grenadine
creator: Constantino Ribalaigua Vert (claimed)
source: Cocktails Bar La Florida (Havana, 1934; 1937, 1939 eds.)
notes: Constante, who told a 1937 interviewer he invented the Presidente, made it with gold Bacardi and a half-spoon of curaçao and no grenadine. Modern specs combine both versions (curaçao plus a barspoon of grenadine).

name: Hotel Nacional Special
variant: Wil P. Taylor's recipe, as given by Charles H. Baker (1939)
creator: Wil P. Taylor
source: Charles H. Baker Jr., The Gentleman's Companion Vol. II (1939)
notes: Baker credits hotel manager Wil Taylor and calls it a Mary Pickford with lime added: gold Bacardi and fresh pineapple sharpened with lime and scented with apricot brandy. Donn Beach's pineapple-and-apricot rum drinks sit right next to it.

name: Mai Tai Swizzle
variant: 1933, Don's Beachcomber Café (per Phoebe Beach)
creator: Donn Beach
source: Phoebe Beach & Arnold Bitner, Hawaii: Tropical Rum Drinks & Cuisine by Don the Beachcomber (2001), as cited in Wikipedia's Mai Tai article; recalled, not re-verified online in this session
notes: Beach's widow said this swizzle was on his 1933 menu, which would predate Trader Vic's 1944 Mai Tai. Historians see little in common beyond the name. Its grapefruit, falernum, Cointreau, Pernod and bitters are classic Beachcomber seasoning, and the 1933 date is disputed.

name: Planter's Punch
variant: Bar La Florida (El Floridita), Havana, 1934 menu book
creator: Constantino Ribalaigua Vert
glass: champagne saucer filled with cracked ice
source: Cocktails Bar La Florida (Havana, 1934; same in 1935/1937 eds.)
notes: Havana's take on the Jamaican punch: dark Jamaica rum sharpened with lime and seasoned with a spoon each of curaçao and grenadine, poured unstrained over cracked ice with fruit. Curaçao-plus-grenadine seasoning reappears in many early tiki punches.

name: Golden Glove
variant: Bar La Florida 'Floridita Style' (1934/1937)
garnish: orange peel expressed over the top
source: Cocktails Bar La Florida (Havana, 1934; 1937 ed.)
notes: A Jamaican-rum Daiquiri No. 4 with Cointreau, electric-blended and finished with orange oil — an early pairing of funky Jamaican rum with orange liqueur that the Mai Tai would make famous.

name: Hotel Nacional Special
variant: 'National Cocktail', Bar La Florida (1934–1939) — no lime
source: Cocktails Bar La Florida (1934, 1935, 1939 eds.); 1948 Club de Cantineros manual adds 'drops of lime'
notes: Havana's bar books print the 'National' as half rum and a quarter each of pineapple and apricot brandy, with no lime — a much sweeter, apricot-forward drink than Baker's Hotel Nacional Special. The 1935 Old Waldorf version instead uses equal rum and pineapple with a dash of apricot.

name: Hula-Hula
variant: Ray Buhen, Beverly Hills Hotel, 1934 (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
creator: Ray Buhen
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: Created by the Filipino bartender who later founded the Tiki-Ti (1961), in his first bar job. An equal-parts gin, curaçao and orange juice cocktail with no added citrus acid, closer to an Orange Blossom than a tiki sour.

name: Planter's Punch
variant: As mixed at the Angostura Bar, Port of Spain, Trinidad (Angostura Recipes, 1934)
source: Angostura Recipes — 42 Cocktails (Angostura-Wuppermann, 1934), 'Planter's Punch as mixed at Angostura Bar, Trinidad'
notes: A Trinidadian house version of the 1-2-3 rum punch, with a full teaspoon of Angostura and nutmeg on top; the cracked ice supplies the 'four of weak'. Its heavy bitters dose is the ancestor of the Angostura-crowned Queen's Park Swizzle.

name: Sumatra Kula
variant: c. 1934, Don the Beachcomber (Berry)
creator: Donn Beach
source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007): amounts recalled, not re-verified online in this session
notes: One of Beach's earliest menu drinks: a light-rum Daiquiri stretched with orange and grapefruit and sweetened with honey. It shows the three-citrus-plus-honey template that later carried the Navy Grog. Amounts are unverified; the ingredient list is solid.

name: Zombie
variant: 1934, Don the Beachcomber (Berry decode, Sippin' Safari)
creator: Donn Beach

ingredients.orig: Don's Mix (2 parts white grapefruit juice : 1 part cinnamon syrup)

glass: tall chimney (Zombie) glass, topped up with ice cubes
source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007), decoded from a Don the Beachcomber bartender's notebook
notes: The drink that launched tiki: three rums over a lime and grapefruit-cinnamon sour, with falernum and a spoon of grenadine for sweetness and anise plus bitters as seasoning. Beach hid the recipe behind coded bottles; Berry's 2007 decode replaced decades of guesswork. Flash-blended for a few seconds only and famously limited to two per customer.

name: Honolulu
variant: Trader Vic's (Bartender's Guide, rev. 1972, 'one of the first drinks we ever originated')
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: fresh pineapple (about half a slice), blended

source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972) via Make and Drink transcription and Difford's adaptation
notes: A blended pink pineapple daiquiri that Vic marked with his TV logo and said was among the very first drinks the Oakland bar originated. It is unrelated to the older gin-based Honolulu Cocktail.

name: Shark's Tooth
variant: Trader Vic's No. 1 (Bartender's Guide, rev. 1972: 'one of the first drinks we ever made')
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: Vic's own Shark's Tooth, distinct from Don the Beachcomber's, is a strong rum rickey with both lemon and lime, a touch of grenadine and soda. Vic said it was among the first drinks made at Hinky Dink's.

name: Beachcomber's Gold
variant: 1937, Hollywood & Palm Springs version (Berry)
creator: Donn Beach
glass: cocktail glass lined with a shaved-ice shell
source: Jeff Berry (Grog Log / Beachbum Berry Remixed), 1937 Hollywood & Palm Springs version
notes: A three-rum Daiquiri seasoned with Pernod and a few drops of almond extract, strained into a cocktail glass lined with a shell of shaved ice. A later, simpler house version paired rum with dry and sweet vermouth.

name: Cobra's Fang
variant: c. 1937, Don the Beachcomber (Berry, Total Tiki)
creator: Donn Beach
source: Jeff Berry, Total Tiki app (earlier: Grog Log / Remixed)
notes: A single-rum knockout: a full 1.5 oz of 151 Demerara over lime, orange and passion-fruit syrup, seasoned with falernum, bitters and absinthe. The original called for Passionola, the ancestor of fassionola. The falernum dose differs between Berry's editions (1/4 vs 1/2 oz).

name: Q.B. Cooler
variant: c. 1937, Don the Beachcomber (Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed)
creator: Donn Beach
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010)
notes: Three rums with orange, lime, honey, falernum and a touch of ginger, lengthened with soda. Some historians argue it is a Mai Tai precursor. A later Mai-Kai version swaps in fassionola, Pernod and grenadine for the ginger.

name: Vicious Virgin
variant: c. 1937, Don the Beachcomber
creator: Donn Beach
source: Donn Beach's recipe as reproduced by Kitchen Riffs (2016) and the Cocktail Party app
notes: A two-rum frappé Daiquiri with Cointreau and falernum as the only sweeteners, blended with cracked ice and served in a freezer-chilled champagne glass. The Virgin Islands rum inspired the name. The Mai-Kai later served a descendant, the Impatient Virgin.

name: Daiquiri No. 5
variant: Bar La Florida (El Floridita) 1939 — 'Pink' Daiquiri
creator: Constantino Ribalaigua Vert
source: Bar La Florida — Cuña del Daiquirí Cocktail (Havana, 1939)
notes: No. 4 tinted pink with a spoon of grenadine, electric-blended with powdered ice. It first appears in the 1939 booklet.

name: Havana Special
variant: Bar La Florida (1939)
source: Bar La Florida — Cuña del Daiquirí Cocktail (1939); Floridita Cocktails (1939)
notes: Rum and pineapple in equal parts with a spoon of sugar, shaken hard and strained — the plainest of the Havana pineapple cocktails. Sloppy Joe's (1939–40) served a different Havana Special of equal rum, pineapple and Cointreau.

name: Hemingway Daiquiri
variant: 'E. Hemingway Special', Bar La Florida (1939)
creator: Constantino Ribalaigua Vert (for Ernest Hemingway)
source: Bar La Florida — Cuña del Daiquirí Cocktail (1939); Floridita Cocktails (1939)
notes: Daiquiri No. 3 with the sugar left out, for a customer famous for disliking sweet drinks. Later retellings (the 'Papa Doble') double the rum and add more grapefruit; the 1939 menu is the earliest printed spec.

name: Hemingway Daiquiri
variant: IBA official 'Hemingway Special' spec (modern)
source: IBA official cocktail list (Contemporary Classics)
notes: The modern codified Hemingway: grapefruit becomes a major juice and maraschino the only sweetener, giving a bittersweet, pale-pink sour served up.

name: Mulata Daiquiri
variant: Bar La Florida (1939) — original with Elixir Bacardí

ingredients.orig: 1/2 oz Elixir Bacardí (plum-infused rum liqueur, defunct; modern specs use dark crème de cacao)

source: Bar La Florida — Cuña del Daiquirí Cocktail (1939); Manual de Coctelería (Havana, 1959)
notes: The 'dark' Daiquiri: aged Bacardi with Elixir Bacardí, a sweet plum-rum liqueur that vanished when Bacardi left Cuba; since the 1970s bartenders substitute crème de cacao, which is how it is mapped here.

name: Zamboanga 'Zeinie'
variant: Charles H. Baker Jr., The Gentleman's Companion (1939)
source: Charles H. Baker Jr., The Gentleman's Companion Vol. II (1939), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: One of Baker's colonial-Pacific finds, which he said travelled down the islands from Manila to Mindanao: a brandy sour with pineapple syrup, maraschino and bitters. Difford's adaptation adds saline, left out here; Baker's original amounts weren't checked.

name: Hurricane
variant: Pat O'Brien's 1940s original (Jeff Berry's reconstruction)
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010), as quoted by Moody Mixologist and others
notes: Invented to clear out cases of unpopular rum the bar was made to buy before its distributor would sell it whiskey. The pre-mix drink was just rum, lemon and passion-fruit syrup at 4:2:2, which amounts to an oversized passion-fruit sour on dark rum. Nobody wrote the original down; Berry's 4:2:2 is the accepted reconstruction.

name: Mahukona
variant: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946)

ingredients.orig: 2 dashes Angostura, put in the glass first and left unstirred
Puerto Rican rum (Ron Merito or Brugal)

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), p. 56, as quoted by the Food Timeline; later in the 1972 guide
notes: A light, lower-proof pineapple-lemon rum sour that Vic said he had served for years, from a recipe scribbled on a scrap of paper whose origin he had forgotten. The bitters go into the glass first and are left unmixed, so they come through as a streak.

name: Missionary's Downfall
variant: Don the Beachcomber (Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed)
creator: Donn Beach

ingredients.orig: 1/4 cup mint leaves, tightly packed (blended in)

source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010)
notes: A frozen, bright-green Daiquiri: fresh pineapple and a big handful of mint are blended with rum, honey and a half-shot of peach brandy (about 20 seconds). It appears on 1940s Beachcomber menus, and Berry suggests it may go back to 1937.

name: Pago Pago
variant: The How and When (c. 1940) via Berry's Remixed
source: Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010), after Gale & Marco's The How and When (c. 1940), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: A pre-war pineapple daiquiri accented with green Chartreuse and white crème de cacao; Berry traces it to a c. 1940 bar book rather than to Trader Vic. Sources disagree on the liqueurs (0.5/0.5 at Difford's; Anders Erickson uses 1/4 oz Chartreuse and 1/2 oz cacao; a Ronrico booklet version reverses that).

name: Navy Grog
variant: c. 1941, Don the Beachcomber (Berry)
creator: Donn Beach

ingredients.orig: honey mix (equal parts clover honey and hot water)

glass: double old-fashioned, around a shaved-ice cone
garnish: shaved-ice cone frozen around a drinking straw
source: Jeff Berry (Grog Log / Beachbum Berry Remixed), Don the Beachcomber spec
notes: Beach's upgrade of the Royal Navy ration: three rums (light, Jamaican, Demerara) with equal parts lime and grapefruit, sweetened with honey and lengthened with a little soda. It is served around a cone of shaved ice with the straw frozen inside. Trader Vic later answered with an allspice-accented Navy Grog of his own.

name: Test Pilot
variant: c. 1941, Don the Beachcomber (Berry)
creator: Donn Beach
source: Jeff Berry, Grog Log (1998) / Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010)
notes: A short, strong two-rum sour sweetened by Cointreau and falernum rather than syrup, with Beach's Pernod-and-Angostura seasoning. It led to the Space Pilot and, most famously, the Luau's Jet Pilot.

name: Kava Bowl
variant: Trader Vic c. 1942 (Berry, Intoxica!), single-serve adaptation
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Difford's Guide adaptation of the Trader Vic recipe in Jeff Berry's Intoxica! (2002)
notes: A pineapple-lemon light-rum punch named after the Polynesian kava ceremony, which also inspired Vic's communal Scorpion bowls. Only Difford's single-serve adaptation was available, so the original bowl proportions are unconfirmed.

name: Suffering Bastard
variant: 1942, Joe Scialom (from his papers, via Berry, Remixed)
creator: Joe Scialom
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010), from Scialom papers lent by his daughter Colette
notes: A wartime hangover cure for Allied officers: gin and brandy with lime cordial, bitters and ginger beer. The IBA and Smuggler's Cove use 0.5 oz fresh lime (Smuggler's adds 0.25 oz demerara syrup), and bourbon often replaces the brandy. Unrelated to Trader Vic's later rum drink of the same name.

name: Three Dots and a Dash
variant: WWII era, Don the Beachcomber (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
creator: Donn Beach
garnish: three cherries and a pineapple chunk speared together (Morse 'V')
source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: A wartime drink named for Morse code 'V' for Victory, which the garnish spells out with three cherries and a pineapple spear. Aged Martinique rhum leads, with a little Demerara, and falernum plus allspice dram give it a baking-spice finish over lime, orange and honey.

name: Mai Tai
variant: 1944 original, Trader Vic's Oakland (17-year J. Wray & Nephew)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: juice of one fresh lime (one spent shell kept for garnish)

source: Victor Bergeron's own published account of the 1944 formula (as quoted in Trader Vic's later writings and by Jeff Berry)
notes: Vic built this in 1944 around a single aged Jamaican rum, using orgeat and orange curaçao as a nutty-orange sweetener pair and only a quarter ounce of rock candy syrup. Shaken with shaved ice and dumped unstrained, the spent lime shell and mint sprig are meant to look like an island with a palm tree. Don the Beachcomber later claimed the drink derived from his Q.B. Cooler, a claim Vic disputed.

name: Doctor Funk
variant: Trader Vic's version, Book of Food and Drink (1946)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: dark Jamaica or Martinique rum (Red Heart, Myers's or Rum Negrita)
1 lime, halved and squeezed; shells dropped into the shaker

garnish: fruit or a fresh geranium leaf
source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), p. 54, as quoted by the Food Timeline
notes: Named for Dr. Bernard Funk, the German physician in Samoa whose absinthe, grenadine and lime tonic appears in South Seas travel writing. Vic's version is a strong dark-rum punch with a quarter ounce of Pernod, both lemon and lime, and a soda top.

name: El Diablo
variant: 'Mexican El Diablo', Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: juice of 1/2 lime; squeezed shell dropped in the glass

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), in Smuggler's Cove's reading
notes: One of the earliest tequila highballs in an American bar book: tequila, lime and crème de cassis topped with ginger ale over cracked ice. It later became a modern-classic standard, usually made with ginger beer.

name: Fog Cutter
variant: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946) / Bartender's Guide (1947)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: Puerto Rican rum (Ron Merito, Boca Chica or Brugal)

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), via the Food Timeline; same spec in the 1947 and 1972 Bartender's Guides
notes: Rum, brandy and gin stacked on a lemon-heavy orgeat base, with a sherry float that adds a nutty top note. Vic warned it was a 'triple threat', and the 1972 guide added his line that after two of these you won't even see the fog.

name: Planter's Punch
variant: Trader Vic's own version, Book of Food and Drink (1946)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), p. 61, as quoted by the Food Timeline
notes: Vic's personal Planter's Punch is a strong one, with 3 oz of dark Jamaican rum, lime plus lemon, and grenadine as nearly the only sweetener. It is stirred with large ice, poured over cracked ice and topped with soda.

name: Scorpion
variant: 1946 punch-bowl recipe for about 12 (Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: 1 1/2 bottles Puerto Rican rum (Ron Merito or Brugal); fifth-size bottles assumed
2 sprigs mint, steeped with the punch

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), p. 77, as quoted by the Food Timeline
notes: Vic's first printed Scorpion is a make-ahead punch: rum with a little gin and brandy, lots of lemon, orange and orgeat, stretched with white wine and left on cracked ice for two hours. He credited the idea to a Honolulu punch originally made with okolehao (ti-root spirit).

name: Shingle Stain
variant: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: dark Jamaican rum (Red Heart or Myers's)

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), pp. 67-68, as quoted by the Food Timeline
notes: A short, rum-forward sour pairing dark Jamaican and Martinique rum, the same combination Vic later used for the Mai Tai, with a quarter ounce of pimento dram for spice. Almost all the sugar comes from the allspice liqueur and a dash of grenadine.

name: Tortuga
variant: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946) / Bartender's Guide (1947)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: 2 dashes crème de cacao (modern readings: 3/8-1/2 oz)

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946) / Bartender's Guide (1947, unchanged in 1972), via Cocktail Virgin Slut and Vintage American Cocktails
notes: Two overproof rums (Cuban and 151 Demerara) with sweet vermouth, three citrus juices, and chocolate-orange accents from cacao and curaçao. Jeff Berry thinks Vic modeled it on the Havana La Florida cocktail. The book lists the liqueurs as 'dashes', which modern makers read as roughly 3/8 to 1/2 oz each.

name: Trader Vic Punch
variant: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: dark Jamaica rum (Red Heart or Myers's)
Puerto Rican rum (Ron Merito or Brugal)
1 slice pineapple, hand-shaken with the drink

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), p. 69, as quoted by the Food Timeline
notes: Vic's own house rum punch pairs dark Jamaican and light Puerto Rican rum over half an orange and half a lemon, with a pineapple slice and a touch of orgeat. It is shaken by hand with shaved ice and served unstrained, and the orgeat is an early sign of the Mai Tai's flavor pairing.

name: Wahine
variant: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: Puerto Rican rum (Ron Merito, Boca Chica or Brugal)

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), p. 108, as quoted by the Food Timeline
notes: Equal parts rum and pineapple juice over one large piece of ice in a coconut shell, which Vic suggested for hostesses entertaining at luncheon. It is about the simplest possible tropical drink and an early coconut-shell presentation.

name: Zombie
variant: Trader Vic's simplified home version, Book of Food and Drink (1946)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: Puerto Rican rum (Ron Merito or Brugal)

source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), pp. 70-71, as quoted by the Food Timeline
notes: Vic openly credited the Zombie to Don the Beachcomber and printed this simpler version of his own: three rums with a full ounce of orange curaçao, lemon, orange and grenadine instead of Don's secret mixes. It is stirred rather than blended and poured over cracked ice.

name: Banana Cow
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947); Make and Drink transcription and Difford's adaptation
notes: A blended banana-milk rum shake with a dash each of vanilla and Angostura, and Vic's cold variation on the old milk punch. Difford's credits it as a Bergeron creation.

name: Eastern Sour
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: juice of 1/2 orange (shell added to glass)
juice of 1/2 lemon (shell added to glass)

source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947); proportions per Jeff Berry and Make and Drink / Jason Miller readings of the book
notes: A whiskey sour done the Trader Vic way: orange juice lengthens it and a quarter ounce of orgeat plus sugar rounds it out, with the squeezed fruit shells left in the glass. Readings of 'half an orange' range from 1½ to 2½ oz, so the orange amount here is a midpoint.

name: Potted Parrot
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947-72)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: orange curaçao (Difford's adaptation uses triple sec)

glass: Potted Parrot mug or sling glass
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947-72), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: A long light-rum drink that is effectively a Menehune Juice lengthened with orange and lemon, the Mai Tai and Scorpion templates merged. It stayed on Trader Vic's menus for decades, served in a parrot-shaped mug.

name: Periodista
variant: Difford's Guide 'Periodista Daiquiri' (after the 1948 Cuban bartenders' manual)
source: Difford's Guide, 'Periodista Daiquiri'; earliest known print: El Arte del Cantinero (Club de Cantineros, Havana, 1948)
notes: 'The journalist': a Bacardi Daiquiri seasoned with small amounts of apricot brandy and curaçao, first printed in Havana's 1948 bartenders' manual (whose OCR-garbled fractions are hard to read); Boston's revived version uses more lime and liqueur.

name: Samoan Fog Cutter
variant: 1950s lighter, blended version (Berry, Total Tiki)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: cream sherry (e.g. Harvey's Bristol Cream), floated

source: Jeff Berry, Total Tiki / Beachbum Berry Remixed, after Trader Vic c. 1950s
notes: Vic toned down his Fog Cutter by cutting the rum to 1½ oz and the brandy to ½ oz and flash-blending it with crushed ice. It became the version on Trader Vic's menus, served in its own tall ceramic mug.

name: Zombie
variant: c. 1950 version (printed by Louis Spievak, 1950; Berry, Intoxica!)
creator: Donn Beach

ingredients.orig: 1 tsp brown sugar, dissolved in the citrus

source: Jeff Berry, Intoxica! (2002); also Ted Haigh, Vintage Spirits & Forgotten Cocktails; originally published by Louis Spievak (1950)
notes: The Zombie as Beach was pouring it around 1950. There is no Don's Mix, falernum or grenadine; lemon, lime, pineapple and passion fruit syrup carry a lighter three-rum base. This was the best-known 'authentic' Zombie until the 1934 original was decoded.

name: Hawaiian Room
variant: Hotel Lexington, New York (Saucier, Bottoms Up, 1951)
location: New York City, New York, USA
source: Ted Saucier, Bottoms Up (1951); reprinted in Jeff Berry's Grog Log (1998)
notes: The signature of Manhattan's Hawaiian Room, the Hotel Lexington's hula-show supper club from 1937 to 1966: an up cocktail of rum with applejack, triple sec, pineapple and lemon. East Coast 'Hawaiian' rather than Beachcomber style; 1951 is the publication date.

name: Mai Tai
variant: Royal Hawaiian Hotel, 1953 (Trader Vic for Matson); spec from 1956 hotel recipe
creator: Victor Bergeron (Trader Vic)

ingredients.orig: dash of curaçao (dash = 1/4 oz per Vic 1972 guide)

source: 1956 Royal Hawaiian recipe as documented by Kevin Crossman, The Search for the Ultimate Mai Tai (ultimatemaitai.com)
notes: Vic's Hawaiian adaptation replaced the long-aged Jamaican rum with light Puerto Rican plus Myers's and trimmed the sweeteners to equal dashes; it had no pineapple or orange juice. The juice-heavy, dark-rum-float Royal Hawaiian Mai Tai served today is a later evolution.

name: Piña Colada
variant: Caribe Hilton, 1954 (hotel's published recipe)
creator: Ramón 'Monchito' Marrero

ingredients.orig: coconut cream (sweetened cream of coconut, i.e. Coco López)

source: Caribe Hilton / Hilton Stories (hotel's own published recipe: blend with 1/2 cup crushed ice ~15 seconds)
notes: The hotel's own recipe splits the coconut between one part sweet cream of coconut and one part heavy cream, so it is richer and less sugary than most later bar specs, with a big 6 oz of pineapple. Marrero is said to have spent three months on it once canned cream of coconut made the drink practical; some accounts say it was first shaken rather than blended. Puerto Rico made it the official national drink in 1978.

name: Mai Tai
variant: Trader Vic's second formula, 1950s (1 oz Jamaican + 1 oz Martinique rum; Berry, Sippin' Safari)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: gold Jamaican rum (Vic used his own Trader Vic Jamaican)

source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007), after Trader Vic's post-17-year-rum formula (published in Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide, rev. 1972)
notes: When the 17-year Wray & Nephew ran out (and a 15-year stopgap after it), Vic split the rum between a Jamaican and a Martinique rum to imitate its weight and funk. This two-rum Mai Tai is the template most modern bars follow.

name: Scorpion
variant: Individual serving, Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972)
notes: The single-glass Scorpion drops the gin and wine of the 1946 punch and keeps a 2:1 rum-to-brandy base with orange, lemon and orgeat. It is spindle-mixed with a scoop of shaved ice, then poured over ice cubes.

name: Zombie
variant: 1956, Don the Beachcomber Waikiki (Cabaret Quarterly; Berry, Sippin' Safari)
creator: Donn Beach
source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007), from Cabaret Quarterly (1956)
notes: Beach's Hawaii-era Zombie keeps the 1934 skeleton of lime, grapefruit, falernum, grenadine, anise and 151. It adds pineapple and a large dose of maraschino liqueur. Modern tasters often cut the maraschino to 1/4-1/3 oz.

name: Blue Hawaii
variant: 1957, Harry Yee (Hawaiian Village)
creator: Harry Yee
venue: Kaiser's Hawaiian Village Hotel (later Hilton Hawaiian Village)
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: Created when a Bols representative asked Yee for a drink to sell blue curaçao. A pineapple-and-sour base split between rum and vodka; not the same drink as the later cream-of-coconut Blue Hawaiian.

name: Tropical Itch
variant: Harry Yee, Hawaiian Village Hotel (late 1950s)
creator: Harry Yee
source: Harry Yee's recipe as reported by PUNCH / Imbibe (per Jeff Berry, Yee used no juice other than passion fruit)
notes: Yee's long passion-fruit highball on a bourbon-plus-rum base, served with a bamboo backscratcher to take home. The spirits are sometimes given as 1.5 oz amber 151, and later versions add pineapple and lemon.

name: Jet Pilot
variant: The Luau, c. 1958 (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007), p. 130; same spec in Smuggler's Cove (2016), p. 61
notes: Steve Crane's Luau took Don the Beachcomber's Test Pilot frame (lime, grapefruit, cinnamon, falernum, Pernod, bitters) and loaded it with three rums including Lemon Hart 151. Effectively a compact Zombie; blended only about five seconds.

name: Aku-Aku Gold Cup
variant: Aku Aku, Stardust Hotel (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
venue: Aku Aku Polynesian Restaurant, Stardust Hotel

ingredients.orig: 1 tsp sugar, dissolved in the lemon juice

source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: A falernum-sweetened lemon sour on light rum with a Myers's accent, strained over a molded ice shell like the Mai-Kai's.

name: Dead Bastard
variant: Joe Scialom four-spirit escalation (via Berry, Remixed)
creator: Joe Scialom
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010), as made by Cocktail Virgin Slut (2016)
notes: The joke sequel to the Suffering Bastard: four spirits at half an ounce each, so the total alcohol matches the two-spirit original. The Dying Bastard (three spirits) sits between the two.

name: Hawaiian Sunset
variant: Aku Aku, Stardust Hotel (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
venue: Aku Aku Polynesian Restaurant, Stardust Hotel
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007); identical in Smuggler's Cove (2016) p. 62
notes: A vodka sour sweetened with orgeat and a little grenadine, served up. It shows vodka showing up on Polynesian menus by 1960.

name: Kamehameha Rum Punch
variant: Hotel King Kamehameha, Kona
garnish: pineapple chunk speared to a cherry
source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: A pineapple-led rum punch from the Kona hotel, with only a teaspoon each of grenadine, syrup and blackberry brandy. The dark Jamaican rum is floated, so the first sips are rum-heavy.

name: Tiki Bowl
variant: Kon-Tiki, Portland, 1960 (Berry)
source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007); Smuggler's Cove (2016) p. 68 (1 oz honey, 2 dashes Herbstura)
notes: A Kon-Tiki original that copies Donn Beach's signature honey, Pernod and Angostura combination across three rums with orange and lime. The Kon-Tiki chain came from Stephen Crane's 1958 deal with Sheraton to compete with Hilton's Trader Vic's.

name: Chimp in Orbit
variant: Royal Kona Resort recipe cards (Hilton standard)

ingredients.orig: lemon juice as transcribed (may stand in for sweet & sour)

source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007 / 2017 edition)
notes: The name points to the 1961 chimpanzee space flights (hence the circa-1961 date); found among the Royal Kona's old recipe cards. It pairs sweet vermouth and crème de cacao with orange and lemon, which is unusual. Transcriptions disagree on the grenadine, and the large lemon amount may originally have been sweet-and-sour mix.

name: Captain's Grog
variant: Captain's Inn, c. 1962 (Berry, Remixed; same in Smuggler's Cove)
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010); Smuggler's Cove (2016), p. 65
notes: A grog sweetened with maple syrup, a rare tiki sweetener, with vanilla and almond extracts, falernum and curaçao over three rums, lengthened with seltzer.

name: Space Needle
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972) via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription
notes: A big two-rum Mai Tai relative that swaps lime for lemon and doubles the curaçao; the name points to Seattle's 1962 World's Fair, where Trader Vic's had a presence. Date and venue are inferred from the name.

name: Hawaiian Eye
variant: Tony Ramos, China Trader, c. 1963
creator: Tony Ramos
glass: Hawaiian Eye mug or old fashioned
source: Tony Ramos recipe as transcribed by TikiBot; cross-checked against Difford's Guide and Mixing Up Tiki (listed in Berry's Total Tiki)
notes: Made by Tony Ramos at the China Trader for the cast of the TV series Hawaiian Eye and served in a now-collectible mug: a simple falernum daiquiri on gold and light rum. Published versions differ on the lime and the rum split (Difford's adds more falernum and uses rich syrup; Mixing Up Tiki uses 1.5 oz of one rum and 0.75 oz lime).

name: London Sour
variant: 1963, Trader Vic's at the London Hilton (Bartender's Guide, rev. 1972)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: Vic's Scotch counterpart to the Eastern Sour, made for the opening of his London restaurant in the Hilton on Park Lane in 1963. It is orange-dominant and only lightly sweetened with orgeat.

name: Piña Colada
variant: Barrachina, Old San Juan, 1963 (house frozen-base method)
creator: Ramón Portas Mingot

ingredients.orig: rum, a shot poured into the glass first ('to taste')
1 part Coco López or Goya cream of coconut
3/4 part water blended into the base (batch: 48 oz pineapple, 15 oz coconut cream, 10 oz water)

source: Barrachina's house method as reported by The Kitchn (bartender interview) and The Georgetowner (restaurant's batch recipe)
notes: The rival birthplace claim: a plaque at Barrachina credits Mingot with the drink in 1963. Their base is pineapple and cream of coconut at about 4:1, thinned with water and frozen to a slush without ice. Rum goes into the glass first and the slush is poured over it, and there's no dairy. Some retellings say Mingot's first version used condensed milk, but the restaurant's current method doesn't.

name: Lovely Lovely
variant: Papeete Bar, Waikikian Hotel, c. 1964 (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
creator: 'Danny' (Papeete Bar)
venue: Papeete Bar, Tahitian Lanai, Waikikian Hotel

ingredients.orig: 2 tablespoons brown sugar (one transcription reads 2 teaspoons)

source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: A frozen daiquiri built on 151-proof Puerto Rican rum, split lime and lemon, and brown sugar. The sugar reads as 2 tbsp in one transcription and 2 tsp in another; tablespoons fits the 2 oz of citrus.

name: Boo Loo
variant: c. 1965 (Berry; Smuggler's Cove spec)

ingredients.orig: 2 1/2 oz pineapple juice + 6 muddled 1-inch fresh pineapple chunks (~1 1/2 oz)

source: Smuggler's Cove (2016) p. 249, after Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010)
notes: A circa-1965 party drink of unstated origin served in a hollowed-out pineapple with two straws: muddled fresh pineapple, honey and lime under four rums. The rum categories are Smuggler's Cove's.

name: Saturn
variant: 1967, J. 'Popo' Galsini (Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed)
creator: J. 'Popo' Galsini
venue: California Bartenders' Guild entry, IBA world championship (winner)
glass: pilsner (often served in a coupe today)
garnish: lemon peel ring around a cherry
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010)
notes: A rare gin-based tiki classic that won the 1967 world bartending championship: passion fruit, falernum and orgeat over London dry gin. It was originally blended; Smuggler's Cove shakes it with 0.75 oz lemon. The garnish rings a cherry with lemon peel to suggest the planet.

name: Ray's Mistake
variant: Tiki-Ti, 1968: amateur reconstruction (the house recipe is secret)
creator: Ray Buhen
source: Ian Moerson, 'Making Ray's Mistake' (blog, 2016), via teekee-deebee; origin story per Berry, Sippin' Safari
notes: The Tiki-Ti's best-known drink, said to be born when Ray Buhen used the wrong syrups in an Anting Anting. The recipe is still secret, and Jeff Berry reportedly rejects this reconstruction. Only passion fruit and a dark-rum float are widely agreed on.

name: Golden Wave
variant: Joe Yatco, China Trader, 1969
creator: Jose 'Joe' Yatco
source: Difford's Guide (adapted spec); also listed in Berry's Total Tiki
notes: Joe Yatco's 1969 China Trader creation: light rum with orange liqueur and falernum over pineapple and lemon, blended with crushed ice. The proportions are Difford's adaptation and were not checked against Berry's printed version.

name: Aloha Cocktail
variant: Hank Riddle, 1970 competition
creator: Hank Riddle
venue: Don the Beachcomber, Palm Springs (competition entry)
source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: Hank Riddle's entry in a 1970 cocktail competition, made (per the transcription) while he tended bar at the Palm Springs Don the Beachcomber: a served-up rum sour tinted with grenadine and Danish cherry wine and fortified with 151. It was a competition drink, not a Beachcomber menu item.

name: Sweet Dream
variant: Kelbo's, 1970
creator: Hank Riddle
location: Fairfax Avenue, Los Angeles, California, USA
source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: A small creamy dessert drink Hank Riddle made in his final year at Kelbo's: cacao, banana and pineapple with cream and a little light rum, dusted with nutmeg. Closer to a Golden Cadillac than to a sour.

name: Navy Grog
variant: Playboy's Host & Bar Book (Thomas Mario, 1971)
creator: Thomas Mario (published version)
source: Thomas Mario, Playboy's Host & Bar Book (1971), via Make and Drink
notes: A magazine-era Navy Grog with no honey or grapefruit, built on orange, pineapple, guava syrup and falernum instead. It shows how far the name had drifted from Don the Beachcomber's original by the early 1970s.

name: Painkiller
variant: Pusser's 4-1-1 spec, No. 2 strength (after the Soggy Dollar Bar original)
creator: Daphne Henderson
location: White Bay, Jost Van Dyke, British Virgin Islands

ingredients.orig: Pusser's Rum — 2 oz for a No. 2; No. 3 = 3 oz, No. 4 = 4 oz

glass: tall glass or Pusser's enamel tin mug
source: Pusser's Rum official recipe (4 parts pineapple, 1 cream of coconut, 1 orange, rum to taste by number); history via Wikipedia and Chilled Magazine
notes: Created by Daphne Henderson at a swim-up beach bar in the BVI. Pusser's founder Charles Tobias could not get her recipe and reportedly worked up his own match; the company trademarked the name in 1989, so the brand's 4:1:1 ratio with Pusser's is now the reference. It is ordered by number (No. 2, 3 or 4) for the ounces of rum; the No. 4 roughly doubles the strength. Basically a Piña Colada rounded out with orange juice and finished with a heavy nutmeg cap.

name: Rum Runner
variant: Holiday Isle Tiki Bar, 1972 (Tiki John Ebert; as documented by Jeff Berry)
creator: John 'Tiki John' Ebert
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010), p. 56; cross-checked against ultimatemaitai.com 'Perfect Pour Rum Runner' and Food.com 'Holiday Isle Rum Runner' (same fractions)
notes: Ebert made it to use up surplus blackberry brandy, banana liqueur and rum, and named it after the Keys' Prohibition smugglers. The documented original has no pineapple or orange juice. It is a blended, sweet-tart 151 sour where the two fruit liqueurs supply most of the sugar and flavor. One Holiday Isle-attributed variant splits the rum into 1/2 oz Bacardi Black plus 1/2 oz 151. Some sources date it to the 1950s.

name: Scorpion Bowl
variant: Bowl for a group, Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), as summarized by Vintage American Cocktails
notes: The communal Scorpion as served in Trader Vic's restaurants, blended with two scoops of shaved ice and poured into a ceramic bowl with long straws. The book does not give a head count; servings=4 is an estimate by volume (about 2.5 individual Scorpions' worth of liquid before dilution).

name: Tiki Puka Puka
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972); Navy Grog mix reconstructed
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: part of 3 oz Trader Vic Navy Grog Mix (reconstructed)
part of 3 oz Trader Vic Navy Grog Mix (reconstructed)
part of 3 oz Trader Vic Navy Grog Mix (reconstructed)
part of 3 oz Trader Vic Navy Grog Mix (reconstructed)

source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), as reported by Cocktail Virgin Slut; the Navy Grog mix is split using the lime : grapefruit : demerara : pimento ratio of Vic's Navy Grog
notes: Vic's three-rum strong drink (light, dark Jamaican and 151 Demerara) is lengthened with orange juice and his bottled Navy Grog mix, then reddened with grenadine. The published recipe calls for 3 oz of the mix, and its breakdown into lime, grapefruit, demerara syrup and pimento dram here is a reconstruction. Trader Vic's current recipe is different, using orange, lemon, grenadine and only 1 oz of grog mix.

name: Jungle Bird
variant: Kuala Lumpur Hilton original (Poister 1989; Berry, Intoxica 2002)
creator: Jeffrey Ong
source: Kuala Lumpur Hilton recipe via John J. Poister, The New American Bartender's Guide (1989); reprinted by Jeff Berry, Intoxica! (2002)
notes: Beverage manager Jeffrey Ong created it as the welcome drink for the KL Hilton's July 1973 opening; it is often misdated to 1978. The original is a long, pineapple-dominant drink with Campari as the bitter accent. The 2000s craft version (Giuseppe González) cut the pineapple to 1.5 oz and used blackstrap rum.

name: Bushwacker
variant: Blended (standard modern spec)
source: Liquor.com 'Bushwacker' spec (recalled; not re-verified online this session)
notes: A boozy coconut milkshake: coffee and chocolate liqueurs over cream of coconut and milk, blended with dark rum. It started in the Virgin Islands in the mid-1970s and became the house drink of Florida Panhandle beach bars (Pensacola Beach, Flora-Bama). Gulf Coast versions often add a 151 float or ice cream.

name: Hinky Dinks Fizzy
variant: 1984, Trader Vic's 50th anniversary (Smuggler's Cove spec)
creator: Trader Vic's (company)
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove (2016)
notes: Made for Trader Vic's 50th anniversary and named after Hinky Dink's, the Oakland saloon Vic opened in 1934. Gin and rum go over pineapple, passion fruit and apricot, and the drink is poured onto sparkling wine in a snifter.

name: Miami Vice
variant: Frozen Piña Colada and frozen Strawberry Daiquiri poured side by side

ingredients.orig: light rum, 1.5 oz in each half

source: Composite of common published specs (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: Named after the 1980s TV show. Two frozen drinks, a Strawberry Daiquiri and a Piña Colada, are blended separately and poured together, layered or swirled, so the tart strawberry half and the rich coconut half mix as you drink. A cruise-ship and beach-bar staple.

name: Ancient Mariner
variant: Jeff Berry & Annene Kaye, 1994 (Beachbum Berry's Grog Log, 1998)
creator: Jeff "Beachbum" Berry & Annene Kaye
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Grog Log (1998); spec as reproduced by Punch and Difford's Guide
notes: Began as Berry's attempt to reverse-engineer Trader Vic's take on the Navy Grog and ended up as a new drink: a Demerara plus dark-Jamaican rum sour with grapefruit and allspice dram as the signature accent. Named for Coleridge's poem because of how long the tinkering took; the best-known original from the revival's chief historian.

name: Cable Car
variant: Tony Abou-Ganim, Starlight Room, 1996
creator: Tony Abou-Ganim
venue: Starlight Room, Sir Francis Drake Hotel

ingredients.orig: part of 1.5 oz fresh lemon sour (2 lemon : 1 simple)
part of 1.5 oz fresh lemon sour (2 lemon : 1 simple)

source: Tony Abou-Ganim, The Modern Mixologist (2010) (recalled; not re-verified)
notes: A spiced-rum Sidecar with a cinnamon-sugar rim, named for the cable cars running past the Starlight Room. One of the first fresh-citrus signature drinks of the pre-revival 1990s and an early bar use of spiced rum in a balanced sour.

name: Hell in the Pacific
variant: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Grog Log (1998)
creator: Jeff "Beachbum" Berry
garnish: lime wedge speared with small American and Japanese flags
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Grog Log (1998)
notes: Berry's reworking of the 1930s Myrtle Bank Punch from Kingston's Myrtle Bank Hotel: a straight 151-proof Demerara sour sweetened only with maraschino and a little grenadine, shaken with crushed ice and dumped unstrained. The blood-red color and dueling-flags garnish are a nod to the Pacific War.

name: Gin-Gin Mule
variant: Audrey Saunders, 2000
creator: Audrey Saunders
source: Audrey Saunders (Pegu Club house signature); spec as widely reproduced (recalled; not re-verified)
notes: Saunders' cross of a Mojito and a Moscow Mule: muddled mint, lime and sugar shaken with gin and a spicy house ginger beer. Tiki-adjacent rather than tiki, it became a Pegu Club signature and helped make fresh ginger beer a standard back-bar ingredient.

name: Old Cuban
variant: Audrey Saunders, 2001
creator: Audrey Saunders
source: Audrey Saunders (later a Pegu Club signature); spec as widely reproduced (recalled; not re-verified)
notes: A Mojito reworked as an elegant up drink: aged Spanish-style rum, lime, sugar and mint shaken and double-strained, dashed with Angostura and topped with Champagne. Tiki-adjacent rather than tiki, it shares the Queen's Park Swizzle's rum, lime, mint and Angostura core.

name: Porn Star Martini
variant: Douglas Ankrah, Townhouse, London, 2002
creator: Douglas Ankrah
garnish: side shot of Champagne (not mixed in)
source: Douglas Ankrah; spec as widely reproduced (Difford's) (recalled; not re-verified)
notes: A passion-fruit and vanilla vodka sour served with a sidecar shot of Champagne, which is left out of the ingredients here because it is drunk separately. Not tiki, but the most popular tropical-fruit cocktail of the era in Britain; include it or drop it as a tropical-flavor reference point.

name: Chartreuse Swizzle
variant: Marcovaldo Dionysos, c. 2003
creator: Marcovaldo "Marco" Dionysos
source: Marco Dionysos; spec as reproduced by Punch, Kindred Cocktails and Smuggler's Cove (Cate, 2016)
notes: Won Dionysos a Chartreuse-sponsored bartending competition and became a signature of San Francisco's early craft and tiki scene, later a Smuggler's Cove staple (which is why some sources wrongly say it was created there). It makes a 110-proof herbal liqueur the base of a swizzle, with pineapple, lime and falernum doing the tropical work. Some reproductions use 1.5 oz Chartreuse; dates of 2002 and 2003 both circulate.

name: Nuclear Daiquiri
variant: Gregor de Gruyther, LAB, London, 2005
creator: Gregor de Gruyther
source: Gregor de Gruyther, spec as published by Difford's Guide and Punch
notes: Equal parts unaged Jamaican overproof, green Chartreuse and lime, with only a splash of falernum for sugar, so the Chartreuse supplies most of the sweetness. A London cult drink that showed funky rum and falernum could work in a stark, spirit-heavy craft format; the creator's instruction is that no garnish can survive it.

name: China Clipper
variant: Forbidden Island, 2006 (Martin Cate's opening program)
creator: Martin Cate (Forbidden Island)

ingredients.orig: five-spice syrup (1 rounded tsp five-spice powder steeped in 2:1 syrup)
aged amber rum (Cruzan Estate Dark, Appleton V/X, Brugal Añejo, Lemon Hart 80 or Pyrat XO)

source: The Barman Cometh blog (2009); history per Punch
notes: Named for Pan Am's China Clipper flying boat, which began transpacific service from Alameda in 1935. A plain aged-rum sour made distinctive by a rich syrup steeped with Chinese five-spice, typical of the house-made spice syrups (cinnamon, cardamom, five-spice) that set Forbidden Island's program apart.

name: Siesta
variant: Katie Stipe, Flatiron Lounge, 2006
creator: Katie Stipe
source: Katie Stipe; spec as reproduced by Punch (recalled; not re-verified)
notes: A tequila take on the Hemingway Daiquiri, with Campari standing in for maraschino beside lime and grapefruit. Tiki-adjacent: one of the drinks that made bitter-plus-citrus a craft staple around the same time bitter tiki drinks appeared.

name: Trinidad Especial
variant: Valentino Bolognese, 2008
creator: Valentino Bolognese
source: Valentino Bolognese competition recipe, as reproduced by Kindred Cocktails / Difford's (recalled; not re-verified)
notes: The competition-winning drink that first used a full ounce of Angostura as a base alongside pisco, orgeat and lime. Giuseppe González reworked it into the Trinidad Sour (rye and lemon in place of pisco and lime). Exact proportions vary between reproductions.

name: Dead Reckoning
variant: Martin Cate, c. 2008–09 (pre-Smuggler's Cove)
creator: Martin Cate
location: San Francisco Bay Area, California, USA

ingredients.orig: premium aged rum (Cockspur 12 or Flor de Caña 12)

source: Martin Cate, as published on the Tikidrinks blog (Aug 2009) and Cocktail Virgin (2010); later in Smuggler's Cove (2016)
notes: A competition-winning Cate original from between his Forbidden Island years and the opening of Smuggler's Cove. Aged rum is stretched with lemon and pineapple, sweetened with maple syrup, vanilla-cognac liqueur and tawny port, then lengthened with soda. It shows Cate's habit of using fortified wine and non-cane sweeteners as the hidden modifier layer.

name: Flor de Jerez
variant: Joaquín Simó, Death & Co, c. 2009
creator: Joaquín Simó
source: Death & Co: Modern Classic Cocktails (2014) (recalled; not re-verified)
notes: A low-proof sour in which amontillado sherry is the base and Jamaican rum only a modifier, with apricot liqueur and Angostura giving the fruit-and-spice lift of a tiki sour. Only loosely tiki: an early Death & Co example of sherry and rum working together.

name: Jungle Bird
variant: Giuseppe González re-spec, New York, c. 2009–10 (less pineapple, blackstrap rum)
creator: Giuseppe González (after Jeffrey Ong, 1978)
source: Giuseppe González re-spec as widely reproduced in the craft era (recalled; not re-verified)
notes: González found the 1978 Kuala Lumpur Hilton drink in Berry's Intoxica and rebuilt it for the craft bar: the pineapple is cut from about 4 oz to 1.5 oz and a molasses-heavy blackstrap rum replaces generic dark Jamaican. Campari now reads as a bitter backbone rather than a tint, and this shorter spec is the one most bars now serve.

name: Kingston Negroni
variant: Joaquín Simó, Death & Co, 2009
creator: Joaquín Simó
source: Joaquín Simó (Death & Co menu, spring 2010); spec as reproduced by Punch and Death & Co
notes: An equal-parts Negroni with navy-strength Smith & Cross in place of gin, reportedly worked out within minutes of Simó first tasting that rum. Carpano Antica was picked because it has the body to stand up to the rum's esters. Created in 2009 and on Death & Co's menu from spring 2010, it made funky Jamaican pot-still rum a normal base for stirred bitter drinks.

name: Mezcal Mule
variant: Jim Meehan, PDT, late 2000s
creator: Jim Meehan
source: Jim Meehan, The PDT Cocktail Book (2011) (recalled; not re-verified)
notes: A mule rebuilt around smoky mezcal, unsweetened passion fruit purée and muddled cucumber, finished with a dusting of chili. An early example of mezcal and tropical fruit together in a craft bar, a few years before mezcal tiki became common. Amounts of agave and ginger beer are approximate.

name: Trinidad Sour
variant: Giuseppe González, Clover Club, 2009
creator: Giuseppe González
source: Giuseppe González; spec as published by Difford's Guide and Punch
notes: Turns the usual proportions upside down: a full 1.5 oz of Angostura is the base and rye is only the modifier, with orgeat and lemon taming it into a nutty, spiced sour. Grew out of Valentino Bolognese's competition-winning Trinidad Especial and became the model for bitters-as-base drinks.

name: Undead Gentleman
variant: Martin Cate, Smuggler's Cove
creator: Martin Cate
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove (2016); spec as reproduced by Grouchy Bartender, Jolly Bartender and Cocktail Virgin
notes: The 1934 Zombie condensed into an up drink: the same lime, grapefruit, cinnamon, falernum and Angostura skeleton, minus grenadine, over aged and black overproof rums, served in an absinthe-rinsed coupe instead of with Pernod drops. Spec is solid, but the creation year is approximate: it may date from Smuggler's Cove's early years rather than its 2009 opening.

name: Tia Mia
variant: Ivy Mix, Lani Kai, 2010
creator: Ivy Mix
source: Ivy Mix, Spirits of Latin America (2020); Imbibe
notes: A split-base Mai Tai where mezcal shares the base with Jamaican rum, created for the opening of Julie Reiner's Lani Kai and named for a woman Mix knew in Guatemala. One of the first widely copied drinks to put smoky agave into the Mai Tai template. Created 2010, just after the revival window.

name: Bitter Mai Tai
creator: Jeremy Oertel
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 130
notes: Moves Campari from modifier to base (1.5 oz) and keeps a Mai Tai frame of lime, orgeat and curaçao, with navy-strength Jamaican rum as the backbone. It became the template for amaro-based Mai Tai riffs.

name: Lost Lake
creator: Paul McGee
source: Matt Pietrek & Carrie Smith, Minimalist Tiki (2019), p. 240
notes: The house drink of Paul McGee and Shelby Allison's Chicago bar. Jamaican rum with passion fruit, pineapple and lime, and quarter-ounce accents of maraschino and Campari that add depth without making it bitter.

name: Hurricane
variant: Smuggler's Cove craft spec (Martin Cate)
creator: Martin Cate (restoration of the 1940s formula)
garnish: cocktail umbrella speared into a lemon wedge
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove (2016)
notes: Cate keeps the three-ingredient 4:2:2 structure but uses molasses-heavy black blended rum and flash-blends it with 12 oz crushed ice plus a few agitator cubes. This is the fresh-ingredient Hurricane craft tiki bars point to when they reject the red mix.

name: 151 Swizzle
variant: Don the Beachcomber (Berry)
creator: Donn Beach
glass: frosted metal swizzle cup or pilsner
source: Jeff Berry (Grog Log / Beachbum Berry Remixed), Don the Beachcomber spec (recalled; not re-verified)
notes: A one-rum swizzle: 1.5 oz of 151 Demerara with lime and sugar, seasoned with Beach's usual Angostura and drops of Pernod, churned over crushed ice until the cup frosts, then topped with nutmeg. The Mai-Kai kept a close relative on its menu for decades. Proportions are recalled, not checked.

name: 151 Swizzle
variant: Mai-Kai version, Atomic Grog tribute reconstruction
source: The Atomic Grog (Hurricane Hayward) tribute recipe, as made by Make and Drink (YouTube)
notes: The Mai-Kai's take on the Beachcomber 151 Swizzle adds falernum, grenadine and a little dark Jamaican to the overproof Demerara base.

name: Aku Aku
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), Smuggler's Cove adaptation
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: blended lightly aged rum (orig. light rum)

garnish: large mint leaf or small mint sprig cluster
source: Smuggler's Cove (2016), adapting Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972); cross-checked with Difford's
notes: A blended, double-strained pineapple-mint daiquiri with a little peach, close kin to Don the Beachcomber's Missionary's Downfall. It is served up, which is unusual for a tiki drink.

name: Almost Famous
creator: Shannon Mustipher
location: New York City, New York, USA
source: Shannon Mustipher, Tiki: Modern Tropical Cocktails (2019), p. 47
notes: The equal-parts Naked and Famous (a Last Word descendant) with unaged, high-ester Jamaican overproof in place of mezcal. The funky rum does the job the smoke did.

name: Amaro di Cocco
creator: Ryan Lotz
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 117
notes: A Negroni-colada hybrid with Campari and sweet vermouth in equal parts, rum, and a colada body, and no citrus at all. Pineapple and the bitter aperitivo provide the acidity and edge.

name: Angostura Colada
creator: Zac Overman
source: Matt Pietrek & Carrie Smith, Minimalist Tiki (2019), p. 211
notes: A widely copied modern colada with Angostura bitters as the base and half an ounce of Smith & Cross for backbone. The heavy clove-cinnamon bitterness takes the place of the usual rum.

name: Après-Ski Swizzle
creator: Nathan Hazard
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 126
notes: Light Barbados rum with three-quarters of an ounce of green Chartreuse, pineapple and orgeat; related to the Chartreuse Swizzle. The powdered-sugar garnish is meant to look like snow.

name: Bahama Mama
variant: Classic bar-guide spec with coffee liqueur
source: Gary Regan, The Bartender's Bible (1991) / Webtender spec (recalled; not re-verified online this session)
notes: The older printed Bahama Mama is a long pineapple drink with three small rum pours (dark, coconut, 151) and a quarter-ounce of coffee liqueur, which adds a faint roasted note under the fruit. The Bahamian origin story is folklore; the drink spread through cruise ships and resort bars.

name: Bahama Mama
variant: Modern cruise/resort version (coconut rum, orange, grenadine)
source: Composite of common cruise-line and chain-restaurant specs (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: The Bahama Mama most vacationers are served drops the coffee liqueur and 151. It is coconut rum and dark rum stretched with equal pineapple and orange and tinted with grenadine, with no fresh citrus at all, so sweetness depends entirely on the juices. Representative proportions only; this is a composite of common specs.

name: Bajan Rum Punch
variant: Barbados, 'one of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak'
source: Traditional Barbadian proportion rhyme, as served in Bajan hotels and rum shops (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: The Barbados form of the Caribbean punch rhyme is plain water, not juice, for the 'weak', finished with Angostura and nutmeg. That makes it a drier, rum-forward punch that shows off Bajan rum. Recorded in rhyme parts as ounces, making two servings; the 'water' ID is proposed in resort.new-ingredients.json.

name: Baldwin's (Easy) Sherry Colada
creator: Ran Duan
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 109
notes: A low-proof colada with two ounces of amontillado sherry as the whole base. Lemon keeps it from turning cloying, and the nutty, saline sherry pairs well with coconut.

name: Bali Bali
variant: Bali Ha'i at the Beach, New Orleans (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
venue: Bali Ha'i at the Beach (Pontchartrain Beach)
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: A four-spirit tall punch (Jamaican and light rum, gin, Cognac) over a three-juice, passion and falernum base, from the amusement-park Polynesian restaurant at Pontchartrain Beach.

name: Bali Hai
variant: House of Happy Talk, Hanalei Plantation, early 1960s (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
venue: House of Happy Talk, Hanalei Plantation

ingredients.orig: Hanalei house mix (2 oz total: 3 lemon : 1 each orange, pineapple, guava nectar, orgeat : 1/4 each passion fruit juice, simple)

source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007), from the California Bartenders Guild magazine Good Taste; house-mix proportions per teekee-deebee
notes: A sparkling hotel punch: rum and a lemon-heavy house juice mix topped with Champagne. Another version uses okolehao, lime, lemon and simple syrup, so the spec is uncertain. The mix is expanded into its parts here.

name: Banana Daiquiri
variant: Frozen resort style (St. Thomas tradition)
source: Composite of common resort specs (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: A whole ripe banana turns the frozen daiquiri thick and custardy, and a little banana liqueur backs it up. The Mountain Top lookout on St. Thomas advertises itself as the home of the original. Proportions here are representative, not a documented house spec.

name: Barrel O' Rum
variant: Mai-Kai signature, Atomic Grog tribute reconstruction
creator: Mariano Licudine
source: The Atomic Grog (Jim 'Hurricane' Hayward) tribute recipe, as made by Make and Drink (YouTube)
notes: The Mai-Kai's house signature, likely a descendant of Don the Beachcomber's Rum Barrel; the real recipe is secret. A second Atomic Grog-derived version (Mixing Up Tiki) uses 2 oz each of lime, orange, grapefruit and passion syrup with only 1 tsp honey, so proportions are uncertain.

name: Beachbum's Own
variant: Jeff Berry, created to christen Bosko Hrnjak's Beachbum tiki mug
creator: Jeff "Beachbum" Berry
glass: tiki mug (Bosko Beachbum mug) or tall glass
source: Jeff Berry recipe as reproduced by Rumdood (2010) and the Cocktail Party app
notes: Berry wrote this to launch the tiki mug sculptor Bosko Hrnjak made in his likeness. Unusually for Berry, the vanilla-citrus of Licor 43 stands in for the usual falernum or allspice spice layer, over an even split of lemon, orange, pineapple and passion fruit and a light-plus-Demerara rum base.

name: Beachcomber
variant: Official Mixer's Manual (Duffy, 1956 ed.) — not Don the Beachcomber's
source: Patrick Gavin Duffy, The Official Mixer's Manual (1956 edition), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: Not a Don the Beachcomber recipe: a Cuban-style daiquiri variant sweetened only with triple sec and a touch of maraschino, from mid-century bar manuals. Difford's lists an optional half teaspoon of rich syrup, left out here.

name: Beachcomber's Gold
variant: later rum-and-vermouth version (commonly printed)
creator: Donn Beach
glass: cocktail glass lined with crushed/shaved ice
source: Bar None Drinks / Absolut Drinks rum-and-vermouth Beachcomber's Gold (weak secondary sources, seen via search extracts)
notes: The simpler Beachcomber's Gold with no citrus that shows up in general bar guides: light rum split between dry and sweet vermouth (effectively a rum Perfect Manhattan), served in or over a shell of crushed ice. It probably reflects a later house simplification of the 1937 three-rum original, and the attribution to Beach himself is unconfirmed.

name: Black Magic
variant: Mai-Kai, Atomic Grog tribute reconstruction
creator: Mariano Licudine
source: The Atomic Grog (Hurricane Hayward) tribute recipe, as made by Make and Drink (YouTube)
notes: A secret Mai-Kai coffee drink; this tribute layers four rums over coffee, honey, citrus, falernum and allspice. The coffee-plus-spice idea follows Mariano's earlier Jamoca.

name: Blue Hawaiian
variant: Blended resort version
source: Liquor.com 'Blue Hawaiian' (recalled; not re-verified online this session)
notes: Not to be confused with Harry Yee's Blue Hawaii (1957, sweet-and-sour, no coconut). The Blue Hawaiian crosses that drink with the Piña Colada and is effectively a blue colada. The curaçao adds orange-peel sweetness and color, which pushes the pineapple ratio lower than in a standard colada.

name: Bourbon Special
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription; also listed in Berry's Total Tiki
notes: A short bourbon sour spiced with falernum and Angostura and topped with a splash of ginger beer. It shows how Vic applied tiki modifiers to whiskey for customers who didn't drink rum.

name: Breakfast Mai Tai
creator: Fanny Chu
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 135
notes: Banana and cinnamon replace curaçao to give a 'banana bread' Mai Tai. The black pot-still rum goes in after the shake as a dark top layer.

name: Bumboat
creator: Smuggler's Cove staff
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove: Exotic Cocktails, Rum, and the Cult of Tiki (2016), p. 252
notes: Rye and two rums over a pineapple-lemon-cinnamon base, with drops of almond extract instead of orgeat so the almond note arrives without extra sugar. A bumboat was the small craft that sold provisions to ships at anchor.

name: Cherie Valentino
variant: Kelbo's 'Lovers Utopian Bowl' (Berry reconstruction)
location: Fairfax Avenue, Los Angeles, California, USA
source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007) — Berry's reconstruction
notes: A communal bowl for two served at Kelbo's from the 1950s to the 1980s. A magazine feature listed only the ingredients, so the proportions are Berry's reconstruction, not a recovered spec: a sweet-tart red gin punch with blackberry and grenadine.

name: Chi Chi
