variant: Vodka colada (common bar-guide spec)
source: Common bar-guide spec (e.g. The Bartender's Bible / Webtender); recalled, not re-verified this session
notes: A Piña Colada made with vodka, popular in Hawaiian hotel bars. With a neutral spirit, pineapple and coconut carry all the flavor. Published specs cluster around 1.5 oz vodka, 1–2 oz cream of coconut and 3–4 oz pineapple.

name: Cobra
variant: Kon-Tiki, Chicago (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: A small, very strong single-rum drink: one ounce of 151 Demerara over equal parts lime, orange and passion fruit syrup, sharpened with Pernod and bitters, then topped with crushed ice.

name: Coco No Coco
creator: Ezra Star
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 118
notes: A colada made without coconut: orgeat and heavy cream supply the nutty richness and a short shake keeps the cream from over-aerating. Aged Demerara rum gives it a dessert-like depth.

name: Colonel Beach's Plantation Punch
variant: 1950s, The Colonel's Plantation Beefsteak & Coffee House, Waikiki (Berry)
creator: Donn Beach
venue: The Colonel's Plantation Beefsteak and Coffee House
source: Jeff Berry (Don the Beachcomber Hawaii-era spec), as reproduced by Cocktail Virgin Slut
notes: Beach's Hawaii-era Planter's Punch, made for his Colonel's Plantation restaurant in Waikiki. It has three rums with pineapple, lime and falernum, seasoned with Pernod and Angostura. Pouring it over ginger beer turns the punch into a cooler.

name: Colonial Grog
creator: Garret Richard
location: New York City, New York, USA

ingredients.orig: Ron Navazos Palazzi Oloroso Cask Strength

source: Garret Richard & Ben Schaffer, Tropical Standard (2023), p. 123
notes: A New England–flavored grog sweetened with maple and seasoned with allspice, using dry vermouth for dilution and structure alongside sherry-cask rums. Served around an ice mold, like the Navy Grog's ice cone.

name: Corn 'n' Oil
variant: Smuggler's Cove spec

ingredients.orig: 2 oz blended aged rum (Barbados); blackstrap rum is also common
1/2 oz John D. Taylor's Velvet Falernum

source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove (2016); Difford's Guide 'Corn 'n' Oil'
notes: A Barbadian planters' dram of rum and falernum with bitters, named (per Difford's) for a line in Deuteronomy about corn, wine and oil; it was popularized on the Velvet Falernum back label. It is the prototype of the spirit-forward rum-and-spice 'stirred' tropicals.

name: Cou-Cou-Comber
variant: Joe Scialom, Caribe Hilton (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
creator: Joe Scialom

ingredients.orig: served in (and eaten from) a hollowed-out cucumber

source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: Scialom's post-Cairo gimmick for Hilton in the late 1950s: a dry vodka sour with Pernod, served in a cucumber you eat as you drink.

name: Day of the Dead
creator: Rod Moore
source: Matt Pietrek & Carrie Smith, Minimalist Tiki (2019), p. 257
notes: A Zombie-style heavyweight with three rums including a 151, Pernod drops and allspice, and a softer body from cream of coconut and orange juice. Topped with seltzer.

name: Derby Daiquiri
variant: Mai-Kai, Mariano Licudine (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
creator: Mariano Licudine
glass: cocktail glass set with a Spanish-comb ice shell
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: A frozen daiquiri where orange juice outweighs the lime, served in a coupe framed by one of the Mai-Kai's molded ice shells. The Mai-Kai (opened 1956) kept many Beachcomber techniques alive under ex-Don bartender Mariano Licudine.

name: Dirty Banana
variant: Jamaican resort version
source: Composite of common Jamaican resort specs (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: The favorite blended drink of Jamaica's all-inclusive resorts, built on two island exports, gold rum and Tia Maria, blended with ripe banana and milk. Many bars add banana liqueur, cream or ice cream. With no citrus at all it belongs with the creamy coladas, not the sours.

name: Donga Punch
variant: Don the Beachcomber, 1930s (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
creator: Donn Beach
source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007): ingredient list confirmed (VinePair, Kindred Cocktails); amounts recalled, not re-verified
notes: A three-ingredient showcase for Don's Mix: Martinique rum, lime and the grapefruit-cinnamon blend. It reads like a stripped-down Zombie. The ingredients are confirmed, but the proportions come from memory.

name: Dorado Beachcomber
variant: Dorado Beach Hotel, Puerto Rico (Berry adaptation)
source: Dorado Beach Hotel recipe as adapted by Jeff Berry, via Mixing Up Tiki
notes: A Mai Tai-shaped house drink from the Dorado Beach Hotel in Puerto Rico, built on lemon rather than lime, with orgeat, curaçao and demerara syrup over an overproof and an aged rum. Known only through Berry's adaptation; the exact rums are uncertain.

name: Elusive Dreams
creator: Demi Natoli
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 98
notes: A tiki drink served up: pineapple rum and light rum with pineapple juice, cinnamon and banana, shaken hard and fine-strained into a coupe. It shows modern bars putting tiki flavors in a daiquiri format.

name: For Pete's Sake
creator: Smuggler's Cove staff
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove: Exotic Cocktails, Rum, and the Cult of Tiki (2016), p. 145
notes: Peruvian pisco made tropical with hibiscus and Cherry Heering; an example of tiki structure carried onto an unaged grape brandy. The house hibiscus liqueur is recorded here as hibiscus syrup.

name: Full Fathom Five
creator: Garret Richard
location: New York City, New York, USA
source: Garret Richard & Ben Schaffer, Tropical Standard (2023), p. 181
notes: Built on Don the Beachcomber's buttery Gardenia Mix (as in the Pearl Diver) with three rums, falernum and orange; tart calamansi is used to adjust the acidity.

name: Golden Barnacle
creator: Shannon Mustipher
location: New York City, New York, USA
source: Shannon Mustipher, Tiki: Modern Tropical Cocktails (2019), p. 101
notes: Agricole and Jamaican pot-still rum with Don the Beachcomber's grapefruit–cinnamon combination and a heavy half ounce of pimento dram. Honey rounds it out.

name: Good Enough Gatsby
creator: Sean Quinn
location: New York City, New York, USA
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 151
notes: High-proof bourbon and pear eau-de-vie with pineapple and cinnamon, plus a teaspoon of Fernet-Branca for a bitter, minty edge. The pear brandy is recorded as generic brandy.

name: Goombay Smash
variant: Copycat of Miss Emily's Blue Bee Bar recipe (the original is a family secret)
creator: Emily Cooper ('Miss Emily')
location: New Plymouth, Green Turtle Cay, Abaco, Bahamas
source: Common copycat recipes of the Blue Bee Bar drink (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: The signature of a tiny Out Island bar, sold by the jug, with the formula kept in the family. Copycats agree on coconut rum, a second darker rum, a little apricot brandy and a lot of pineapple. Treat the proportions as a reconstruction.

name: Halekulani Cocktail
variant: House Without a Key, Halekulani Hotel, c. 1930s (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
venue: House Without a Key, Halekulani Hotel

ingredients.orig: sugar syrup (in Smuggler's Cove spec; absent from one Sippin' Safari transcription)

source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007); Smuggler's Cove (2016) p. 61
notes: A pre-war Waikiki hotel sour: bourbon with a three-juice mix (lemon, orange, pineapple), grenadine and bitters, served up. A whiskey drink in tropical dress rather than a rum drink.

name: Hanalei Rum Punch
variant: House of Happy Talk, Hanalei Plantation, early 1960s (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
venue: House of Happy Talk, Hanalei Plantation
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007); house-mix proportions per teekee-deebee
notes: Fresh pineapple and banana blended with the Hanalei house mix, curaçao and rum, poured over ice and finished with a spoon of dark rum. It shares its uncertain house mix with the hotel's Bali Hai.

name: Heavens Above
variant: Top of Toronto (via Berry's Intoxica!)
source: Difford's Guide, adapted from Jeff Berry's Intoxica! (2002)
notes: A Canadian entry in Intoxica!: a long rum-and-pineapple drink with small amounts of chocolate and coffee liqueur. Difford's dates it to about 1970 at the Top of Toronto, but places that restaurant in the CN Tower, which opened in 1976, so the date is unclear.

name: Hitler's Jitters
variant: Café Plaza, Maracaibo (Potions of the Caribbean)
creator: F. García Bode
source: Jeff Berry, Potions of the Caribbean (2013), via Make and Drink
notes: A WWII-era Venezuelan daiquiri variant from Berry's Potions of the Caribbean, flavored with crème de cacao. The 3 oz rum pour comes from a single adaptation and wasn't checked against the book.

name: Honi Honi
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide, rev. 1972 (Mai Tai template with bourbon)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972); proportions follow Vic's Mai Tai template (Difford's adaptation trims the lime)
notes: The name means 'kiss kiss'; it is Vic's Mai Tai skeleton with bourbon swapped in for rum. Vic ran several spirit-swap versions of the Mai Tai (bourbon, tequila, light rum), and this is the whiskey one.

name: Hot Brown Cow
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription
notes: Equal parts hot milk and strong coffee spiked with Jamaican rum and dusted with nutmeg: a café-au-lait version of the Rum Cow, and unsweetened.

name: Hot Rum Cow
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription
notes: Hot milk, light rum, sugar and a dash each of vanilla and Angostura, frothed in the spindle mixer and topped with nutmeg. It is the hot form of Vic's Rum Cow.

name: Hot Zombie
variant: Ron Rico rum company booklet
source: Ron Rico rum company recipe booklet, via Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: A cold-weather version from a Puerto Rican rum brand's promotional booklet: the Zombie's rum, lime, pineapple and passion fruit topped with boiling water and enriched with butter and brown sugar, like a fruity hot buttered rum.

name: Hurricane
variant: Modern two-rum fresh-juice version (as widely published, e.g. Liquor.com)
source: Liquor.com 'Hurricane' (fresh-ingredient version); the 2/2/2/1 core is repeated by many recipe sites. Lime/simple/grenadine amounts recalled, not re-verified
notes: The version most people now make from scratch. Passion fruit comes from juice or nectar rather than syrup, and orange juice and grenadine rebuild the fruitiness and red color the bottled mix gave. It is much juicier and less tart than the 1940s formula. Published amounts vary a lot (orange 1–2 oz, lime 0.5–1 oz).

name: Hurricane
variant: Pat O'Brien's today: 4 oz amber rum + 4 oz house Hurricane mix (mix mapped to real ingredients)

ingredients.orig: part of 4 oz Pat O'Brien's Hurricane Mix (red passion-fruit punch mix) — mapped
part of Hurricane Mix (citric tartness) — mapped
part of Hurricane Mix (red color, cherry-like sweetness) — mapped

glass: large (24 oz) Pat O'Brien's hurricane glass
source: Pat O'Brien's house spec (equal parts amber rum and Hurricane mix over cracked ice) as reported by Country Roads Magazine, Edible Times and Liquor & Drink; the breakdown of the mix is our own approximation
notes: What the courtyard bar actually pours: equal parts amber rum and its own red passion-fruit mix over cracked ice, a shortcut adopted once demand outgrew hand-squeezing. Critics call it 'red-flavored'. The mix is modeled here as sweetened passion-fruit nectar with a little lemon and grenadine, so the proportions are approximate, but the 1:1 rum-to-mix structure (4 oz rum) is documented.

name: Iron Ranger
creator: Erick Castro
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 104
notes: A bourbon sour made tropical with pineapple and falernum and served over crushed ice; an often-cited example of whiskey tiki. It is whip-shaken with a single cube, poured and topped with crushed ice.

name: Island to Islay Punch
creator: Taylor Rae Adorno
location: New York City, New York, USA
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 147
notes: Barbados rum with half an ounce of peated Islay whisky for smoke, over an unsweetened passion fruit and cinnamon sour. It uses peated Scotch as a smoky accent, a common craft-era move.

name: Jamoca
variant: Mariano Licudine (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
creator: Mariano Licudine
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007), p. 144
notes: Coffee as a tiki modifier, a Mariano Licudine signature later seen in the Mai-Kai's Black Magic. The coffee syrup is mapped to brown-sugar syrup since the drink already carries brewed coffee.

name: Jasper's Jamaican Planter's Punch
variant: Jasper LeFranc, Bay Roc Hotel (via Ted Haigh / Stephen Remsberg)
creator: Jasper LeFranc

ingredients.orig: Jasper's Secret Mix share: juice of 12 limes per batch
Jasper's Secret Mix share: 1 1/2 cups sugar per batch
Jasper's Secret Mix share: 1 1/4 oz Angostura per batch

source: Ted Haigh, Vintage Spirits and Forgotten Cocktails (2004); also taught by Jeff Berry
notes: Equal parts dark Jamaican rum and a pre-batched 'secret mix' of lime, sugar, Angostura and a heavy hand of nutmeg — effectively a homemade falernum. The batch mix is converted here to a per-drink share; the hotel-bar date is uncertain.

name: Juan Ho Royale
creator: Smuggler's Cove staff
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove: Exotic Cocktails, Rum, and the Cult of Tiki (2016), p. 119
notes: A rare agave drink on the Smuggler's Cove list: blanco tequila with orgeat, falernum and blue curaçao, served up and topped with sparkling wine. The 'royale' means the sparkling top.

name: Kaiteur Swizzle
creator: Smuggler's Cove staff
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove: Exotic Cocktails, Rum, and the Cult of Tiki (2016), p. 140
notes: Named for Guyana's Kaieteur Falls, so the base is aged Demerara rum. A four-ingredient swizzle that pairs maple syrup with falernum, a Smuggler's Cove habit.

name: Kama'aina
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription
notes: A gin-and-coconut cooler lifted with 7-Up. The name is Hawaiian for a long-time island resident. It shows Vic's later habit of combining cream of coconut with citrus and soda.

name: Kentucky Mai Tai
creator: Dan Sabo

ingredients.orig: Giffard Crème de Pêche de Vigne

source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 133
notes: No rum at all: bourbon and mezcal split the base, and Cynar plus peach liqueur replace curaçao. Lemon rather than lime keeps it softer, showing the Mai Tai frame working on whiskey and agave.

name: Kill Devyl Reef
creator: Shannon Mustipher
location: New York City, New York, USA

ingredients.orig: 0.5 oz honey (undiluted), recorded as 1 oz 1:1 honey syrup

source: Shannon Mustipher, Tiki: Modern Tropical Cocktails (2019), p. 80
notes: Three rums from three traditions (Demerara, Guadeloupe, Jamaica) with unsweetened passion fruit, honey and allspice dram. 'Kill-devil' was an early colonial name for rum.

name: Kiruna Cooler
creator: Garret Richard
location: New York City, New York, USA

ingredients.orig: coconut mix (house blend of cream of coconut and coconut milk)

source: Garret Richard & Ben Schaffer, Tropical Standard (2023), p. 165
notes: A savory coconut cooler that splits the base between dill aquavit and two light rums; sharing its name with a town in Swedish Lapland. The dill-coconut pairing is the book's example of pushing tiki toward savory flavors.

name: Kon-Tiki Mai Tai
variant: Kon-Tiki, Cleveland (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: Shows how far 'Mai Tai' drifted outside Trader Vic's bars: no orgeat or curaçao, instead a Beachcomber-style honey, orange, ginger and Pernod build. Useful as a name-versus-structure outlier.

name: Lady of Singapore
variant: Kon-Tiki, Portland (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: A creamy blended pineapple-coconut drink with dairy and a touch of grenadine, a Kon-Tiki cousin of the Piña Colada from the same era.

name: Last Rites
variant: Mai-Kai, Mariano Licudine (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
creator: Mariano Licudine
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: Three ounces of aged Martinique rum with only light passion fruit and falernum sweetening: a very spirit-heavy Mai-Kai sour.

name: Lava Flow
variant: Hawaiian resort style

ingredients.orig: 2 oz strawberries, muddled with the rums

source: Liquor.com 'Lava Flow' (recalled; not re-verified online this session)
notes: The strawberries are muddled with the rums and poured into the glass first. A banana-pineapple-coconut blend goes in on top, so red streaks push up through the white like lava. Underneath the show it is a banana Piña Colada with a strawberry base; a fixture of Hawaiian hotel bars and luaus.

name: Lei Lani Volcano
variant: Disney's Polynesian Village Resort, 1970s
location: Walt Disney World, Lake Buena Vista, Florida, USA
source: Disney Polynesian Village Resort recipe via Make and Drink; original described in Smuggler's Cove (2016) p. 94 (Lei Lani Volcano 2.0)
notes: The 1970s house drink at Walt Disney World's Polynesian resort: coconut rum and guava nectar with pineapple and lime. Smuggler's Cove later rebuilt it as the Lei Lani Volcano 2.0 with aged rum, cream of coconut and guava soda.

name: Lorikeet
creator: Shannon Mustipher
location: New York City, New York, USA
source: Shannon Mustipher, Tiki: Modern Tropical Cocktails (2019), p. 70
notes: A rye tiki cooler: pineapple, banana and cinnamon over spicy rye, with ten dashes of mixed bitters for structure.

name: Mai Sha Roa Na
creator: Anthony Schmidt
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 132
notes: From Martin Cate's San Diego bar False Idol: a Mai Tai skeleton where banana liqueur takes the curaçao slot and macadamia nut syrup the orgeat slot, over an overproof Jamaican base.

name: Mai Tai
variant: Hawaiian resort style (pineapple and orange juice with a dark-rum float)
source: Composite of Hawaiian hotel-bar specs (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: The Mai Tai as served poolside across Hawaii descends from the Royal Hawaiian's 1953 pineapple-and-orange version. Light rum is stretched with juice, lightly sweetened with orgeat and curaçao, and capped with a dark-rum float so the first sips taste strong. Structurally it is a juice-forward resort punch, not the short 1944 sour, which is why it sits in resort-punch with mai-tai as a secondary family.

name: Malibu Bay Breeze
variant: Malibu brand spec
source: Malibu brand recipe (recalled; not re-verified online this session)
notes: Malibu's coconut-rum version of the vodka Bay Breeze, from the Sea Breeze family of 1980s highballs. It is the simplest resort tropical: sweet coconut liqueur, pineapple and tart cranberry built over ice, with no added citrus or syrup.

name: Manta Ray
variant: Garret Richard, Tropical Standard
creator: Garret Richard
location: New York City, New York, USA

ingredients.orig: Giffard Crème de Pêche de Vigne

source: Garret Richard & Ben Schaffer, Tropical Standard (2023), p. 117
notes: Haitian rum and gin with a small amount of coconut, peach, ginger and mint. It is a light, herbal take on coconut rather than a rich colada.

name: Mauna Kea Kiaha
variant: Batik Bar, Mauna Kea Beach Hotel (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
venue: Batik Bar, Mauna Kea Beach Hotel
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: Coconut two ways (sweetened cream and unsweetened milk) with coffee liqueur and no citrus at all, an unusual acid-free resort drink.

name: Menehune Juice
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947-72 editions)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: 1 lime, squeezed over shaved ice; one shell saved
Trader Vic light Puerto Rican rum

source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947, revised 1972), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: A Mai Tai built on light Puerto Rican rum instead of aged Jamaican, so the orgeat and curaçao sit in front. Vic's menu line promised that one sip might let you see a Menehune, the little people of Hawaiian legend.

name: Merciless Virgin
variant: Skipper Kent's, 1942–1967 (Smuggler's Cove spec)
creator: Frank 'Skipper' Kent
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove (2016), p. 67, from the collection of Jacqueline Zumwalt
notes: From Trader Vic's San Francisco rival Skipper Kent: a lemon rum sour sweetened entirely by liqueurs (Cherry Heering, falernum, curaçao). One transcription gives 0.75 oz curaçao instead of 0.25.

name: Monk's Respite
creator: Smuggler's Cove staff
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove: Exotic Cocktails, Rum, and the Cult of Tiki (2016), p. 251
notes: A light gin cooler lengthened with fresh coconut water and seltzer rather than juice, with a quarter ounce of yellow Chartreuse for herbal lift. The name plays on the monks who make Chartreuse.

name: Montego Bay
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972, TV-logo original)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: A Martinique-rum daiquiri with triple sec and bitters, marked in Vic's guide as a house original. The Jamaican name despite the French-island rum is typical of Vic's loose use of Caribbean place names.

name: Moonkist Coconut
variant: Mai-Kai (recipe published in Esquire; adapted by Make and Drink)
source: Mai-Kai recipe printed in Esquire, as adapted by Make and Drink (YouTube)
notes: Unsweetened coconut milk plus honey and falernum over three rums: a lighter, spicier coconut drink than the cream-of-coconut colada style.

name: Mr. Bali Hai
variant: Bali Hai restaurant (Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed)
location: Shelter Island, San Diego, California, USA
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010)
notes: The house drink of the Bali Hai on Shelter Island, which is still open: dark and light rum with pineapple and lemon, plus coffee liqueur. Coffee as a tiki modifier shows up again in the Mai-Kai's Jamoca and Black Magic.

name: Mr. Bodi Hai
creator: Nathan Hazard
source: Shannon Mustipher, Tiki: Modern Tropical Cocktails (2019), p. 102
notes: A riff on the Bali Hai restaurant's Mr. Bali Hai, which pairs coffee liqueur with pineapple. Barbados rum, macadamia orgeat and a touch of banana make a lighter, nuttier version.

name: Muertito Vivo
creator: Shannon Mustipher
location: New York City, New York, USA
source: Shannon Mustipher, Tiki: Modern Tropical Cocktails (2019), p. 109
notes: A Don's Mix sour (grapefruit plus cinnamon) with a 151 kicker, with Jägermeister in the modifier slot adding herbal bitterness.

name: Myrtle Bank Punch
variant: As recorded in Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947); Berry reading
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1947) as reprinted by Jeff Berry (from memory of Beachbum Berry Remixed; not re-verified online); Difford's gives a different Jamaican-rum/Heering spec
notes: A Jamaican hotel punch that Vic recorded: a short shot of overproof rum sharpened with lime and grenadine, with a cherry-liqueur float. Vic's books also printed the hotel's Northside Special, which shows how much the Kingston hotel bars shaped his early drinks.

name: Mystery Gardenia
variant: Don the Beachcomber (Berry)
creator: Donn Beach
source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007), as reproduced by Webtender Wiki and BG Reynolds
notes: A creamy, honeyed Daiquiri: light rum and lime blended at high speed with Gardenia Mix, then strained up. It probably gave the mix its name, and it is the simpler single-rum sibling of the Pearl Diver.

name: Navy Grog
variant: Disney's Polynesian Village Resort
location: Walt Disney World, Lake Buena Vista, Florida, USA
source: Cooking With Mickey Around the World (Disney cookbook), via Make and Drink
notes: The Polynesian resort's house Navy Grog stays closer to Don's template (honey, grapefruit, lime, soda) but uses just two rums plus a 151 kick. The creation date is unknown; the recipe comes from a Disney cookbook.

name: Navy Grog
variant: Trader Vic's version (Bartender's Guide rev. / Rum Cookery & Drinkery, 1970s)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: third, lighter blended rum (modern readings use Chairman's Reserve or a light blended rum)

source: Trader Vic's 1970s Navy Grog as reproduced by Anders Erickson and discussed by Vintage American Cocktails / The Lost Tiki Lounge; structure cross-checked with Smuggler's Cove
notes: Where Don the Beachcomber sweetened his Navy Grog with honey and added soda, Vic's version splits the sweetener between demerara syrup and pimento dram, which gives it an allspice edge. At the restaurants it was built from his bottled Navy Grog mix, and it became the best-known grog of the 1960s and 70s.

name: Norwegian Paralysis
creator: Smuggler's Cove staff
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove: Exotic Cocktails, Rum, and the Cult of Tiki (2016), p. 119
notes: An aquavit take on Don the Beachcomber's okolehao-based Polynesian Paralysis: orange, pineapple and lemon with a little orgeat. Caraway and dill stand in for the ti-root spirit.

name: Nui Nui
variant: Don the Beachcomber (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
creator: Donn Beach

ingredients.orig: Don's Spices #4 (decoded by Berry as cinnamon syrup)
Don's Spices #2 (1:1 vanilla syrup + allspice dram)

source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: A single-rum spiced sour. Amber Virgin Islands rum with lime and orange is sweetened entirely by two of Beach's coded 'spices': #4 (cinnamon) and #2 (vanilla plus allspice). Decoding it was one of Berry's hardest puzzles.

name: Pahoehoe
variant: Batik Bar, Mauna Kea Beach Hotel (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
venue: Batik Bar, Mauna Kea Beach Hotel
glass: double old fashioned or small tiki bowl
garnish: flaming lemon shell with sugar cube and 151 rum
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: Rum, passion fruit, lemon and grenadine, the Hurricane's flavor profile in a short glass, finished with a flaming lemon shell. Named for the smooth lava found around the hotel.

name: Paniolo Old-Fashioned
creator: Smuggler's Cove staff
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove: Exotic Cocktails, Rum, and the Cult of Tiki (2016), p. 203
notes: A rum Old Fashioned sweetened with li hing mui (salted dried plum) syrup, a Hawaiian snack flavor; 'paniolo' is the Hawaiian word for cowboy. The salty-sour plum does the work that orange peel and sugar do in the classic.

name: Paradise Lost
creator: Kirk Estopinal
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 96
notes: A light, savory tiki drink from Cane & Table's 'proto-tiki' program: vodka and dry fino sherry split the base and coconut water lengthens it. Bitters dashed on top give the aroma.

name: Pearl Diver
variant: Don the Beachcomber (Berry decode; modern spec as adapted by Smuggler's Cove)
creator: Donn Beach

ingredients.orig: gold Puerto Rican rum (Smuggler's Cove: blended lightly aged rum)
Don's Gardenia Mix (butter, honey, cinnamon syrup, vanilla syrup, allspice dram)

source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007) decode, as adapted in Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove (2016) and reproduced by Punch/Imbibe
notes: An iced take on Hot Buttered Rum. Three rums, orange and lime are blended hard (15-20 s) with Gardenia Mix, a whipped butter-honey-spice batter, then fine-strained over fresh crushed ice. The blending is what emulsifies the butter. Rum proportions here follow the widely printed modern adaptation, not a verified transcription of Berry's card.

name: Penang Punch
creator: Garret Richard
location: New York City, New York, USA
source: Garret Richard & Ben Schaffer, Tropical Standard (2023), p. 50
notes: Richard's flash-blended punch: two light-bodied rums over a mix of four juices with mint and a teaspoon of absinthe. Saline seasoning, which the Tropical Standard adds to nearly every recipe, brightens the fruit.

name: Pieces of Eight
variant: Pieces of Eight restaurant, Marina del Rey, early 1960s

ingredients.orig: rum (one source says aged, another light)

source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010), as summarized by the Cocktail Party app; cross-checked with TikiBot's recipe table
notes: The house drink of a pirate-themed Marina del Rey restaurant in the early 1960s. As transcribed it is a Hurricane-style passion fruit sour; the rum style and whether Berry's spec has more ingredients could not be checked against the book.

name: Pilikia
creator: Shea Hogan
source: Matt Pietrek & Carrie Smith, Minimalist Tiki (2019), p. 257
notes: Raspberry liqueur is the largest spirit-based ingredient, with a small bourbon and mezcal base, blended with basil. 'Pilikia' is Hawaiian for trouble; the smoky garnish echoes the mezcal.

name: Piña Colada
variant: IBA official specification
source: International Bartenders Association official cocktail list (recalled; the IBA page was not reachable this session)
notes: The IBA version is much drier and stronger than the Caribe Hilton original: pineapple only matches the rum, and there's no heavy cream. It is the standard spec in bartending courses and international hotel bars, and a useful low-juice reference point for the colada family.

name: Piña Verde
creator: Erick Castro
source: Erick Castro spec as demonstrated on Make and Drink (YouTube), transcribed in the SBoudrias cocktail index
notes: A Piña Colada with green Chartreuse (55% abv) as the entire base, an early example of the craft-era trend of using an intense liqueur as the main spirit. Lime keeps the herbal liqueur and coconut from being cloying.

name: Piñata
variant: Smuggler's Cove
creator: Smuggler's Cove staff
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove: Exotic Cocktails, Rum, and the Cult of Tiki (2016), p. 252
notes: A pineapple-heavy party drink where a full ounce of ginger liqueur and half an ounce of allspice dram supply the spice. It uses the common Smuggler's Cove pairing of one black rum with one lightly aged rum.

name: Pinky Gonzales
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide, rev. 1972 (tequila Mai Tai)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: rock candy syrup (Make and Drink's reading substitutes agave syrup)

source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972) via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription; cross-checked with Everyday Drinkers' version
notes: Vic's tequila Mai Tai, one of many tequila drinks in his 1972 revised guide, which gave agave spirits far more space than earlier bar books. The 2 : 1 : ½ : ¼ : ¼ proportions are the same as his other spirit-swap Mai Tais.

name: Pino Pepe
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), served in a pineapple shell
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: A frozen rum-and-vodka pineapple drink served in a hollowed pineapple, one of the showpiece presentations of Trader Vic's 1960s and 70s menus. Vodka appears as Vic's menus caught up with American tastes of the time.

name: Planter's Punch
variant: Myers's rum recipe (orange-juice style)
creator: Myers's (Fred L. Myers & Son)
source: Myers's rum promotional recipe, as reproduced by several recipe sites
notes: The brand version that spread the drink across mid-century America: dark Jamaican rum lengthened with orange juice instead of water, a little citrus, sugar and grenadine. Myers's called its rum 'Planters' Punch' brand from 1879, but this card's date is unclear, so year is left blank.

name: Polynesian Guava Daiquiri
variant: Kelbo's, 1950s
creator: Hank Riddle
location: Fairfax Avenue, Los Angeles, California, USA
garnish: maraschino cherry and pineapple chunk on a pick
source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: Neither Polynesian nor a daiquiri: a gin sour made with guava nectar and a spoon of crème de banane, flash-blended. A Hank Riddle house specialty at Kelbo's.

name: Porch Light
creator: Chris Coy
source: Matt Pietrek & Carrie Smith, Minimalist Tiki (2019), p. 276
notes: A modern take on Trader Vic's bourbon-based Port Light: apple brandy and rye with sweet sherry, grenadine and passion fruit, given a silky texture with egg white.

name: Port Light
variant: Kahiki Supper Club version (as presented by Mixing Up Tiki)
source: Mixing Up Tiki (YouTube), Kahiki version, as transcribed in SBoudrias/cocktails
notes: A bourbon, lemon and passion fruit sour, one of the few whiskey drinks on classic tiki menus. Attribution is disputed (one database credits Trader Vic). Smuggler's Cove's modern version uses 2 oz bourbon, 1 oz lemon, 0.75 oz honey, 0.5 oz passion fruit and egg white.

name: Privateer
creator: Chris Vanderginst
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 110
notes: A short tequila sour with passion fruit syrup and pineapple, seasoned with salt the way a margarita is. Torched rosemary supplies the aroma.

name: Quarantine Order
creator: William Prestwood
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 95; also Matt Pietrek & Carrie Smith, Minimalist Tiki (2019)
notes: Three ounces of Jamaican rum over Don the Beachcomber's grapefruit–cinnamon pairing plus passion fruit and heavy Angostura, much like a pared-down Zombie. Easy Tiki and Minimalist Tiki print the same spec.

name: Red Sky at Night
creator: Garret Richard
location: New York City, New York, USA
source: Garret Richard & Ben Schaffer, Tropical Standard (2023), p. 261
notes: A rye drink in the style of Trader Vic's whiskey-passion fruit sours such as the Port Light, with grenadine, honey and egg white for a foamy texture.

name: Rum & Fruit
variant: Ron Rico mixers' guide
source: Ron Rico Official Mixers' Guide (rum company booklet), via Make and Drink
notes: A rum-company booklet daiquiri variant with Bénédictine and a little passion fruit syrup; an early example of an herbal liqueur used with tropical fruit. The booklet's date and exact wording weren't checked.

name: Rum Barrel
variant: Steve Crane (Luau / Kon-Tiki) — per Make and Drink recreation
creator: Stephen Crane (attributed)

ingredients.orig: light rum (transcribed as blended lightly aged)
dark Jamaican rum (transcribed as black blended, Jamaica)

source: Make and Drink recreation ('Steve's Rum Barrel'); Berry's Total Tiki lists a 'Rum Barrel (Steve Crane)'
notes: A Rum Barrel attributed by name to Stephen Crane of the Luau and the Kon-Tiki chain: 4 oz of light and dark rum over four juices, sweetened with honey and passion fruit and dashed with Angostura. Known here only from one video recreation, so the attribution and proportions are unconfirmed.

name: Rum Firewalker
creator: Jason Alexander
source: Shannon Mustipher, Tiki: Modern Tropical Cocktails (2019), p. 119
notes: Three ounces of unaged high-ester Jamaican overproof balanced by Campari, lime and cinnamon syrup in equal ounces. A very strong, bitter-spiced sour.

name: Rum Keg
variant: Trader Vic's, served in a ceramic keg for sharing
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription
notes: A communal punch of mostly light rum with lemon, pineapple, passion fruit and apricot liqueur, served in Trader Vic's small ceramic kegs. The four-serving count comes from the transcription.

name: Rum River Mystic

ingredients.orig: 3 drops Bittermens 'Elemakule Tiki on the ice

source: Matt Pietrek & Carrie Smith, Minimalist Tiki (2019), p. 241
notes: A split rye/rum Manhattan-style drink from Lost Lake, with Byrrh quinquina and Bénédictine; the tiki bitters dropped on the ice give the aroma. An example of a stirred drink on a tiki bar menu.

name: Rum Runner
variant: Modern beach-bar version with pineapple (Difford's Guide spec)
source: Difford's Guide 'Rum Runner' (as summarized in search results; page not directly fetchable)
notes: On beach-bar menus the drink picked up pineapple (often orange as well) and standard-proof rums, with the 151 moved to an optional float and the grenadine sometimes floated for a sunset effect. Difford's version keeps it balanced with a full ounce of lime and uses more banana than blackberry. Keys bars still serve it either shaken or frozen.

name: S.O.S. Mai Tai
creator: Ean Bancroft
garnish: flaming lime shell dusted with cinnamon
source: Shannon Mustipher, Tiki: Modern Tropical Cocktails (2019), p. 120
notes: A Mai Tai built on black Jamaican pot-still rum with a little agricole blanc, served tall with a flaming lime shell. It keeps Trader Vic's Jamaica-plus-Martinique idea using modern rums.

name: Samoan Typhoon
variant: Joe King Sui, Hawaiian Village, Tampa (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
creator: Joe King Sui

ingredients.orig: 1 oz honey (straight), expressed as 1:1 honey mix

source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: A two-serving blended punch from a Florida Polynesian motel restaurant, heavy on lime with honey and passion fruit. The straight honey is doubled here to express it as 1:1 honey mix.

name: Scorpion
variant: Kelbo's (Hank Riddle), Los Angeles, 1950s — single serving
creator: Hank Riddle
location: Fairfax Avenue, Los Angeles, California, USA
source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: Kelbo's individual-sized answer to the Scorpion Bowl: passion fruit syrup joins the orgeat, the rum is dark Jamaican instead of light Puerto Rican, and a little gin backs the cognac. Both transcriptions checked agree.

name: Scorpion Bowl
variant: New England Chinese-restaurant (Polynesian-Chinese) bowl
venue: Polynesian-Chinese restaurants (e.g. Hong Kong, Harvard Square; Kowloon, Saugus)

ingredients.orig: 151 poured into the center 'volcano' well and set alight

glass: ceramic scorpion bowl with center volcano well, long straws
source: Composite of Boston-area restaurant descriptions and home recreations (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: Trader Vic's shareable Scorpion as it survived in New England's Polynesian-Chinese restaurants: a big ceramic bowl of rum, a splash of gin or vodka and brandy, orange juice and almond syrup, with a flaming 151 volcano in the middle and a straw for each person. The house versions are usually premixed and sweeter than Vic's. Treat the proportions as representative.

name: Shark's Tooth
variant: Don the Beachcomber chain (Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed)
creator: Don the Beachcomber (chain)

ingredients.orig: syrup from a jar of maraschino cherries
Jamaican rum, served on the side in a shot glass and poured in by the guest

glass: double old-fashioned, with a sidecar shot glass
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010)
notes: A cherry-tinted pineapple Daiquiri with a bit of theater. One rum is flash-blended into the drink and the Jamaican rum arrives in a shot glass for the guest to pour in. Adaptations date it to the 1960s chain era, but the date is not firm. Not related to Trader Vic's soda-topped Shark's Tooth.

name: Shrunken Skull
variant: Popular 1:1:1:1 spec (Anders Erickson / Mixing Up Tiki)

ingredients.orig: gold Puerto Rican rum (Don Q Gold)

source: Anders Erickson (YouTube), as transcribed in SBoudrias/cocktails
notes: A skull-mug staple of mid-century menus including the Mai-Kai. The widely circulated spec is simply equal parts lime, grenadine, Demerara and gold rum; origin and original proportions are not documented here.

name: Sidewinder's Fang
variant: The Lanai, c. 1960s (Smuggler's Cove spec)
glass: large snifter lined with a spiral orange peel
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove (2016), p. 62 (drink documented in Beachbum Berry Remixed)
notes: A long, sour-sweet passion fruit and citrus rum drink stretched with seltzer, presented with an orange peel carved into a snake. Equal parts lime, orange and passion syrup make it a clean 1:1:1 template.

name: Silver Seas
variant: Mr. Lemon Hart's Tropical Treat booklet

ingredients.orig: Lemon Hart dark rum (transcribed as black blended rum)

source: Mr. Lemon Hart's Tropical Treat (Lemon Hart rum promotional booklet), via Make and Drink
notes: From a Lemon Hart rum promotional booklet: a short Beachcomber-style drink with Passionola (a commercial passion fruit syrup), orange and lime, and heavy dashes of both bitters and Pernod. The booklet's date wasn't confirmed, so the era is a best guess.

name: Sleeping Giant
variant: Lagoon Cocktail Terrace, Coco Palms Resort, c. 1960s (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
venue: Lagoon Cocktail Terrace, Coco Palms Resort
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: An orange-pineapple rum cooler with a little orgeat and sour mix, named for the ridge above the Coco Palms. Very low acid, which is typical of the island resort style.

name: Sleeping Lotus
creator: Sierra Kirk
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 145
notes: A gin, lemon and orgeat sour shaken with mint leaves, from Blair Reynolds's Portland tiki bar. It is a stripped-down example of the orgeat sour carried over to gin.

name: Something Tequila
creator: John Bernard
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 112
notes: A big three-ounce añejo tequila punch with lime, orange, pineapple and passion fruit, like a rum barrel with agave in place of rum. Mapped to reposado, the closest aged tequila in the vocabulary.

name: Song of the Siren
creator: Shannon Mustipher
location: New York City, New York, USA
source: Shannon Mustipher, Tiki: Modern Tropical Cocktails (2019), p. 106
notes: Agricole and mezcal with crème de cacao as the only sweetener, finished with a float of alpine amaro. It combines grassy, smoky, chocolate and bitter notes in one short drink.

name: Southpaw Swizzle
creator: Abigail Gullo
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 116
notes: A lighter swizzle: manzanilla sherry and agricole share the base and coconut water lengthens it, with a Jamaican rum float on top. Salty sherry and grassy cane rum are a common modern pairing.

name: Spectacle Island
creator: Chantal Tseng
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 123
notes: Split-base swizzle of agricole and New England dark rum with green Chartreuse and Madeira and no added syrup; the Chartreuse supplies the sweetness. The Madeira is mapped to the closest oxidized fortified wine.

name: Staycation
creator: Devin Kennedy
location: New York City, New York, USA
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 115
notes: A colada with no pineapple: a full ounce of lemon cuts the cream of coconut, and rye shares the base with Demerara rum. Apricot and passion fruit in small amounts supply the tropical fruit.

name: Strawberry Daiquiri
variant: Frozen, blended with fresh strawberries
source: Representative of common published specs (e.g. Liquor.com, Difford's); recalled, not re-verified this session
notes: The blender-era daiquiri that made rum sours a mass-market vacation drink. Fresh berries add body and sugar, so the syrup can come down slightly from a classic daiquiri. Resort bars usually swap the berries for sweetened strawberry purée or mix, which makes it much sweeter.

name: Swizzle Français
creator: Martin Cate
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove: Exotic Cocktails, Rum, and the Cult of Tiki (2016), p. 136
notes: Essentially a Ti' Punch stretched into a swizzle: aged Martinique rhum, cane syrup and lime with a quarter ounce of allspice dram. It shows how little a strong base spirit needs.

name: Tabu
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972; 'originated in Seattle')
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: A frozen pineapple-lemon drink split between light rum and vodka, which Vic said came from his Seattle restaurant. It is plain and fruity, typical of the vodka-friendly 1960s menus.

name: Tahitian Honey Bee
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972)
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (rev. 1972), as adapted by Difford's Guide
notes: A light-rum honey sour, essentially a rum Bee's Knees made with lemon. Honey was a common Polynesian-bar sweetener, and here it is the only one.

name: Tapa Punch
variant: Royal Kona Resort recipe cards (Hilton standard)

ingredients.orig: dark Jamaican rum (transcribed as black pot still rum)
sweet & sour mix (about 3 oz, inferred from transcription), split
sweet & sour mix (about 3 oz, inferred from transcription), split

source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007 / 2017 edition)
notes: One of the recipe cards Royal Kona beverage director Jeff Isbister found in 2008, believed to be a Hilton house standard carried over from Harry Yee's Hawaiian Village. A big punch heavy on dark rum, with peach brandy. The original sweet-and-sour amount is inferred from the one transcription we could check.

name: Tequi La Banane
creator: Orlando Franklin McCray

ingredients.orig: Giffard Crème de Fruit de la Passion

source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 127
notes: Reposado tequila in an orgeat sour, with quarter ounces of banana and passion fruit liqueur. Served in a julep tin with crushed ice.

name: The Expedition
creator: Martin Cate
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove: Exotic Cocktails, Rum, and the Cult of Tiki (2016), p. 140
notes: Cate's homage to Donn Beach: a dark daiquiri skeleton layered with Don-style cinnamon, honey and vanilla plus a quarter ounce of coffee liqueur. Splitting the base between black rum and bourbon shows how whiskey slots into a Beachcomber spice sour.

name: The Mastadon
creator: Alex Smith
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove: Exotic Cocktails, Rum, and the Cult of Tiki (2016), p. 251
notes: A Smuggler's Cove bartender's showpiece served in a hollowed pineapple: equal bourbon and aged rum carried by a big pineapple and passion fruit base, with vanilla (Licor 43) and maraschino as modifiers. Earlier versions circulated with Tuaca and half the passion fruit.

name: The Naked Ape
creator: Smuggler's Cove staff
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove: Exotic Cocktails, Rum, and the Cult of Tiki (2016), p. 134
notes: A short, dark sour where banana liqueur and cinnamon syrup share the sweetening; the only citrus is half an ounce of lemon, so the drink leans rich. A splash of funky pot-still rum sharpens the black rum base.

name: The Twenty Seventy Swizzle
creator: Martin Cate

ingredients.orig: Herbstura (1 dash of equal parts Angostura and Herbsaint)

source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove: Exotic Cocktails, Rum, and the Cult of Tiki (2016), p. 116
notes: Named for its two rums, Angostura 1919 and Lemon Hart 151 (1919 + 151 = 2070). A split demerara/honey sweetener and allspice dram over a light column rum and a 151 kicker; 'Herbstura' is the bar's premix of Angostura and Herbsaint.

name: There's Always Money in the Banana Stand
creator: Zac Overman
source: Matt Pietrek & Carrie Smith, Minimalist Tiki (2019), p. 212
notes: Uses a full pour of peated Islay Scotch as the tiki base, softened by banana liqueur and cinnamon with herbal Chartreuse and allspice. It shows smoky whisky taking the place of funky Jamaican rum.

name: Third Wave Swizzle
creator: Ryan Lotz
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 111
notes: A gin swizzle built on a Bee's Knees (gin, lemon, honey) with cold-brew coffee and ginger added. The name refers to third-wave specialty coffee.

name: Three Scots and a Dash
creator: Zac Overman
garnish: three cherries on a pineapple spear
source: Matt Pietrek & Carrie Smith, Minimalist Tiki (2019), p. 211
notes: A Scotch version of Don the Beachcomber's Three Dots and a Dash: blended and Islay Scotch plus Drambuie in place of the rum and agricole, with honey, allspice and passion fruit. Whisky slots neatly into the Don honey-allspice template.

name: Tiger Shark
variant: The China Trader, 1950s, per Tony Ramos (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
creator: Tony Ramos (recorded)
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: A three-rum pineapple daiquiri blended briefly and strained. Recorded by ex-Beachcomber bartender Tony Ramos from the China Trader, where the Hawaiian Eye TV crew drank.

name: Tonga Punch
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription
notes: A light-rum orange punch sharpened with both lemon and lime and lightly sweetened with curaçao and grenadine. It is typical of the easygoing citrus punches that filled out Vic's menus.

name: Top Notch Volcano
creator: Smuggler's Cove staff (Martin Cate)

ingredients.orig: blended lightly aged rum (e.g. Denizen Aged White)
blended aged rum (e.g. Diplomático Reserva Exclusiva)

source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove: Exotic Cocktails, Rum, and the Cult of Tiki (2016), p. 134
notes: Smuggler's Cove's sharing bowl, named for the bar's designer Ignacio 'Notch' Gonzalez. Unlike the 1970s Volcano Bowl it is a passion fruit–maraschino daiquiri scaled up for four, flash-blended in two batches and set alight.

name: Trader Vic Grog
variant: Trader Vic's (Berry, Grog Log / Total Tiki)
creator: Victor Bergeron

ingredients.orig: dark Jamaican rum (Smuggler's Cove uses a blended overproof rum)

source: Trader Vic via Jeff Berry (Grog Log, Total Tiki); cross-checked with Martin Cate's spec in Easy Tiki and the TikiBot dataset
notes: Vic's house grog is not a Navy Grog copy: dark rum with equal parts lemon, pineapple and passion fruit syrup, sharpened with a heavy dose of Angostura. It is a simple 2 : 1 : 1 : 1 structure.

name: Tradewinds
variant: Caribbean, 1970s (Berry / Smuggler's Cove)
garnish: lemon wedge with an inside-out cocktail umbrella
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010); Smuggler's Cove (2016) p. 94
notes: A 1970s Caribbean drink Berry revived: apricot liqueur and cream of coconut balanced by a full ounce of lemon over dark and light rum. Smuggler's Cove notes that 2 oz of gin can replace the rums; Anders Erickson uses 1 oz cream of coconut.

name: Trinidadi Issues
creator: Chad Austin
source: Matt Pietrek & Carrie Smith, Minimalist Tiki (2019), p. 152
notes: A Trinidad Sour turned into a swizzle, with an ounce and a half of Angostura, orgeat and cinnamon, and pineapple for body. One of several craft drinks that use Angostura as the base.

name: Tropical Itch
variant: Bali Hai, San Diego (Berry, Sippin' Safari)
location: Shelter Island, San Diego, California, USA
garnish: mango slice speared on a bamboo backscratcher
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry's Sippin' Safari (2007)
notes: A different drink from Harry Yee's Tropical Itch that keeps the backscratcher gimmick: gin and light rum with mango, cinnamon and a hint of almond.

name: Western Sour
variant: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide
creator: Victor Bergeron
source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide via Make and Drink (YouTube) transcription; also listed in Berry's Total Tiki
notes: The counterpart to Vic's Eastern Sour: bourbon lengthened with grapefruit instead of orange and sweetened with falernum instead of orgeat.

name: White Cloud
variant: Mai-Kai (as presented by Make and Drink)
source: Make and Drink (YouTube), catalogued with Sippin' Safari recipes in SBoudrias/cocktails
notes: A small coconut daiquiri with falernum and orange liqueur. Only a secondary transcription was available, so treat the proportions as provisional.

name: Wishful Thinking
creator: Julia McKinley
source: Chloe Frechette & the editors of Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), p. 101
notes: Sloe gin, a liqueur, makes up the largest share of the base, with grassy agricole rhum, a hot ginger syrup, bitters and absinthe. An unusual case of a fruit liqueur as the main spirit in a tiki drink.

name: Yacht Rock
creator: Garret Richard
location: New York City, New York, USA
source: Garret Richard & Ben Schaffer, Tropical Standard (2023), p. 259
notes: A bitter tiki drink pairing Campari with chocolate: two Jamaican rums, crème de cacao, blanc vermouth, orange and lime. It shows a Jungle Bird–style drink with a cacao modifier.

name: Yellow Bird
variant: Caribbean resort version (rum, Galliano, banana, orange, pineapple)
source: Composite of commonly published Caribbean resort specs (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: Named for the Caribbean song 'Yellow Bird', a hit for Arthur Lyman in 1961. The resort version sets Galliano's vanilla-anise and banana liqueur over orange and pineapple, and the result really is yellow. A separate, shorter 'Yellow Bird' sour (rum, Galliano, triple sec, lime) also exists in bar guides and is not this drink.

name: You're Not My Real Trinidad
creator: Kevin Beary
source: Matt Pietrek & Carrie Smith, Minimalist Tiki (2019), p. 186
notes: Uses an ounce and a half of Angostura bitters as the base, as the Trinidad Sour does, inside a colada with PX sherry. Two ounces of cream of coconut balance the bitterness.

name: Zombie
variant: Mid-century bar-guide / chain-restaurant style (apricot brandy, pineapple, orange, 151 float)

ingredients.orig: orange juice (some guides use papaya juice)

source: Representative of mid-century bar guides such as Mr. Boston (recalled; exact spec not re-verified this session)
notes: Before Jeff Berry decoded Don's formula, most drinkers got this bar-guide Zombie: no Don's Mix, falernum or Pernod. Apricot brandy and fruit juice stand in for the secret spice, and a 151 float keeps the drink's knockout reputation. Its descendants still appear on chain and resort menus.
